en: The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra,
Scroll One. By Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si, Te-jin Shi Hong-lu Qing, Suo-guo Gong,
Feeding Three Thousand Households, Invested with Purple Robes, and Posthumously Honored as Si-kong.

Posthumous Title: Da Jian (Great Mirror). Official Title: Da Guang Zhi (Great Vast Wisdom). Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Sacred Site of Ghanavyūha (Part One) Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha, the Bhagavat, dwelt in the world of Ghanavyūha, which transcends the perceptions of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; it is a realm where he sports with the supernormal powers and penetrations, possessing sovereign mastery and unimpededness regarding all phenomena. This world is not the domain traversed by those of external paths, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. He was accompanied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten billion buddha-fields, all of whom had practiced the supreme yoga.
Their names were as follows:

They were headed by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Sarvāstivāda-vādi-pramardaka (The Vanquisher of All Heretical Discourses), Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Sarvabuddhadharmayathābhūta-darśin (The One Who Sees All Buddha-Dharmas as They Truly Are) Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Ārya Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Abhijñārāja (King of Supernatural Powers) Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, Vimukticandra (Moon of Liberation) Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, and Dhṛtivikrama (Vigorous Progress) Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. All had transcended the realms of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and having transformed their basis, they had attained the illusory-like body through the Śūraṅgama and Dharmamegha Samādhis; immeasurable Buddhas had poured water upon their crowns, and they dwelt in lotus palaces detached from the three realms of existence.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha arose from the samādhi known as "The Manifestation of Infinite Colors through the Subtle Agility of the Profound Realm of Self-Awakened Noble Wisdom Abiding in Bliss in the Present Life. He emerged from the Palace of Exquisite Adornments with the Splendor of Imperial Thunderlight and, together with the bodhisattvas, entered the Palace of the Stainless Moon-Treasury, where he ascended the lion throne in the field of Ghanavyūha.

Once the World-Honored One was seated, he surveyed the four quarters; from the radiance-adorned pearl-tuft between his eyebrows, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pure lights issued forth, encircling and reflecting one another to form a net of light.

When this net of light radiates and shines forth, the signs of adornment in all Buddha-fields appear with distinct clarity; as if there were only a single Buddha-field, the exquisite and subtle decorations of all other Buddha-lands are as numerous as motes of dust.
The Ghanavyūha World transcends all other Buddha-lands; it is far removed from the stars, the moon, and the sun, and like the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not composed of atoms.

Within this Ghanavyūha, the Buddhas and their sons, as well as those from other worlds who have come to this assembly, are all like *nirvāṇa* and the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of space.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested the supreme and wondrous deeds of the buddhas and bodhisattvas in that world through his majestic spiritual power, he again surveyed the assembly of bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions with his Buddha-eye and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvadharma-yathābhūta-darśin, saying:
“Sarvadharma-yathābhūta-darśin!

This world is now named Ghanavyūha (Dense Array). Within it, the bodhisattvas, throughout the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and among sentient beings who possess or lack ideation, kindle the fire of wisdom through the power of samādhi. They incinerate craving for form as well as ignorance, transform their basis of existence to attain the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body), and adorn themselves with the supernormal powers of psychic travel and mastery. This body is without apertures or cavities and lacks skeletal substance; it is like the sun, moon, mani-jewels, lightning, Indra’s bow, coral, *hṛtitala*, gold, *campaka* flowers, peacock feathers, the moon, or a reflection in a mirror.

Thus, with this physical body dwelling in the various stages (*bhūmi*), one cultivates the causes of the untainted (*anāsrava*); through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one attains mastery, and by means of the ten inexhaustible vows and dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one obtains a sublime body and comes to the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyasamaya*).

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvabuddhadharmatathatādarśana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will compassionately grant me leave to speak.
The Buddha said to Dr̥ṣṭatattva:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you so as to bring joy to your heart.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvabuddhadharmatathatādarśana, having received the Buddha’s permission, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is it only this Buddha-field that transcends the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as the realm of non-percipient beings?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

From here, passing upward through ten billion buddha-fields, there are the Buddha-field of Brahma-sound, the Buddha-field of Śāla-tree King, and the Buddha-field of Constellation King; beyond such buddha-fields, there are further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields, vast, lofty, and magnificent, adorned by assemblies of bodhisattvas.

Therein, all those Buddhas, acting as bodhisattvas, expound for them the Dharma of the ultimate great nirvāṇa realm—the self-realized noble wisdom of dwelling in happiness in the present life, which is free from discrimination and is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) and suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, you should know that beyond this realm there are such immeasurable Buddha-fields. Yathārthadarśin!

It is not only you who have now conceived a limited perception regarding the Buddha-lands and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas and questioned the Tathāgata about them; there was once a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Dhāraṇīśvara who, having likewise conceived a limited perception toward the Buddha, ascended by means of his supernormal powers to the upper direction, passing through hundreds of thousands of koṭis and even as many worlds as the sands of the Ganges, yet he was unable to see even the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
A sense of wonder arose in his mind as he realized that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.

He returned to the great city named Yaśasvī in the Sahā world, where he came before me to repent for his past transgressions and to praise the immeasurable and boundless merits of the Buddha, which are like space; having established himself in the realm of self-realization, he then proceeded to the Ghanavyūha realm.

At that time, in the assembly, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha—who was well-able to expound the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), with subtle, definitive, and exhaustive mastery of their source and depth—rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“I wish to inquire briefly of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I only pray that you will compassionately explain this for me.
The Buddha said, “Vajragarbha!
“If you have any questions regarding what you desire to know from me, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will expound it for you according to whatever you doubt.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, having received the Buddha’s permission, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of the term "Buddha"?
What is that which is awakened?

I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain the realm of ultimate truth and reveal the Buddha of the Dharma-nature, so that those who have practiced, are practicing, or will practice the Bodhisattva path in the past, future, and present may abandon all views that accumulate upon various forms and characteristics, as well as the objective realms of conceptualization adhered to by other heterodox outsiders—namely, such views as atoms, the supreme Lord (Īśvara), primordial nature (Prakṛti), time, direction, space, the self, the mind, and the conjunction of sense organs and objects.

Furthermore, there are those who calculate that ignorance, craving, karma, the eye, forms, and the visual faculty—along with contact and mental attention at that time—such dharmas as these acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), combine to produce consciousness. These practitioners, clinging to this, give rise to various evil conceptions regarding existence and non-existence within my Dharma.
Furthermore, there are some people who, regarding the aggregates and sentient beings, fall into the view of emptiness.

To sever such false conceptualizations, we pray that the World-Honored One will explain the meaning realized by the Great Bodhi of the Buddha—the one who possesses supreme mastery over all phenomena—which is free from the five kinds of characteristics known by consciousness. May those who hear this attain realization according to their understanding of the five kinds of objects of knowledge and thereby achieve perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!"

Possessing mastery over the ten stages and transcending the realm of conceptual discrimination, you have great wisdom and desire to reveal this most excellent yoga of the Buddha-seed, which is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

It is not only you who now conceive a sense of wonder regarding the meaning realized in the Buddha’s enlightenment and question me about it; there are immeasurable sons of the Buddha, such as Bhadramāyākāra and others, who all likewise conceive a sense of wonder regarding this meaning and seek the essence of the Buddha through various forms of reflection and discernment, asking:
"What is the meaning of the term 'Tathāgata'?"
"Is form the Tathāgata? Or is the Tathāgata something other than form?

In this manner, searching internally and externally among the aggregates, elements, bases, and all conditioned phenomena, one does not perceive a Tathāgata, because all such things are of a nature that is subject to destruction and disintegration.
The Tathāgata does not exist within the aggregates; even when analyzed down to the ultimate atom, he is nowhere to be seen.

Why is this? Because when one observes with focused concentration and sublime wisdom, nothing is perceived; because the aggregates are coarse and base; and because the Tathāgata is the eternal Dharma-body.
Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are able to skillfully enter the profound realm of reality (dharmadhātu).
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now speak for your sake.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied, “So be it,” and received the instruction.
The Buddha said, “Good son!

The Tathāgata Vajragarbha, Sovereign of Supreme Samādhi, is neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; he does not rely upon the aggregates nor does he not rely upon them; he is neither arising nor ceasing; he is neither wisdom nor the object of knowledge; he is neither the sense faculties nor their objects.

Why is this? Because the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects are all base and contemptible; one should not perceive the Tathāgata through either the internal or the external.

Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is devoid of cognition and lacks volition; having arisen, it must necessarily perish. It is like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles—merely an accumulation of atoms forming a mass of foam that constitutes the Tathāgata.

Feeling arises from the conjunction of two factors; it is like the perception of water bubbles, jars, or garments, produced by the causal conditions of the conjunction of two factors, and is like a mirage.

For example, when the heat of the earth rises and billows upward, the sunlight shining upon it appears like waves upon water; thus, various birds and beasts, driven by thirst, perceive it as real water when viewing it from afar.

Perception is likewise: it has no intrinsic nature and is false and unreal. For one who possesses discerning wisdom, although there may appear to be a nature, distinct characteristics, and names that can be apprehended, the practitioner of meditative concentration observes them closely as being like a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman—merely provisional designations. Just as forms in a dream are seen falsely through perception alone and are found not to exist upon awakening, so too within the dream of ignorance one sees various forms such as men and women; yet upon attaining perfect enlightenment, nothing at all is seen.
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are like the plantain tree, lacking any solid core; apart from the body and its objects, they have no intrinsic nature.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like a magical illusion, false and unreal. It is, for example, like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, relying on grass, wood, tiles, and pebbles, manifests forms and images, conjuring up people, elephants, horses, and various other figures complete with all their ornaments; yet these are merely objects of craving for the deluded, not for those of true wisdom.

Consciousness is likewise dependent on other factors for its abiding; through pervasive conceptualization, the two types of grasping—the grasper and the grasped—arise. If one realizes this for oneself, they are all transformed and extinguished; therefore, it lacks intrinsic substance and is identical to a phantom person.
Vajragarbha! The Tathāgata is eternally abiding and forever immutable; this object of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Just as space is indestructible and cannot be extinguished, it is called the realm of nirvāṇa and also the *dharmadhātu*.

Because all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, present, and future, have taught in accordance with this, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this nature remains eternally constant; it is called the nature of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the nature of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātutā*), and the nature of the limit of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*).
Vajragarbha! For what reason is it called *niyama*?
Because it is far removed from all faults pertaining to future existence.
Furthermore, this samādhi is able to definitively eliminate all evils pertaining to future existence; for this reason, it is called *niyama*.

If there are those who abide in this samādhi, their minds harbor no attachment toward sentient beings, and they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as well as nirvāṇa. Just as red-hot iron is cast into cold water, they abandon sentient beings; therefore, bodhisattvas relinquish [nirvāṇa] and do not realize it [prematurely].

Why is this? Because they have abandoned great diligence, great compassion, and the various perfections; they sever the lineage of the Buddhas and take to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, treading the paths of heterodox views and false doctrines.
It is just as an old elephant sinking into the mud, submerged by the mire of *samādhi*.

The realm of savoring meditative concentration is likewise; it causes one to regress from all the Buddha-dharma gates and prevents entry into ultimate wisdom. Therefore, the Bodhisattva relinquishes it and does not realize it, remaining merely in a state of proximity.

Entering the Buddha’s Dharma-body with ultimate wisdom, awakening to the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata, one shall attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma; taking the manifold forms of the realm of wisdom as sustenance, one enters the Tathāgata-samādhi and dwells within the sphere of nirvāṇa.

All the Tathāgatas cause them to arise from meditative absorption, whereby they gradually apply themselves to practice and transcend the eighth stage, skillfully making definitive discernments up to the Cloud of Dharma stage. They enjoy the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgatas and enter the stage of the Buddhas’ internal realization. In conjunction with the samādhi of the path of effortless spontaneity, they travel everywhere throughout the ten directions without moving from their original place, while constantly relying upon the Ghanavyūha Buddha-field.

Vajra-Svāmin possesses great transformations; he manifests buddha-fields and achieves mastery, turning the wisdom-samādhi that is the basis of existence, and is fully endowed with the power and supernormal knowledges of the mind-made body, his gait and majestic virtue being like those of the king of geese.

Just as the reflection of the bright moon appears throughout all waters, so too is the Buddha; he universally manifests his physical form according to the needs of sentient beings, ensuring that the benefit bestowed upon all assemblies is never in vain, and further causes them to eventually reach the Pure Land of Ghanavyūha.

According to their inclinations and desires, they gradually guide and entice them by describing all the blissful abodes, such as the palaces of the celestial kings of the desire realm and the pure maṇi-jewel treasuries of sovereign bodhisattvas, as well as the successive stages of the grounds, and manifesting the splendor of wealth, joy, and merit as they travel from one buddha-field to another, responding to the capacities of beings until the end of the future.
It is just as when accomplished vidyādhara-siddhas, various ṛṣis, and the deities of celestial palaces move about among people yet remain invisible;
likewise, when the Tathāgata has completed the deeds performed through his transformations, he abides in his true body, hidden and unmanifested.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The aggregates of the sense-faculties are like a cluster of snakes; They are touched by the conditions of objective spheres.
Born from ignorance, craving, and karma, The bonds of habitual perfuming are difficult to untie."
The evil thoughts of the mind and mental factors coil and entwine like a coiled dragon;
from them, the venom of anger is bestowed, blazing like a fiercely burning fire.
All practitioners of contemplation should constantly observe in this manner.
Because one has relinquished all phenomena of the aggregates, one remains single-minded and untiring.
Just as there may be a shadow in the midst of empty space where no tree exists,
or as the tracks of a horse on a windswept path— such sights are all considered difficult to perceive.
Whether among the primary elements or their derivatives, within form or the formless— should one seek to see the Tathāgata therein,
the difficulty is likewise so great. This applies equally to true suchness (*tathatā*),
the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas.
The practice of internal realization is not within the realm of words.
Nirvāṇa is called Buddha, and Buddha is also called Nirvāṇa;
being free from the discrimination of subject and object, how could it be seen?
When gold ore is crushed into powder, the gold is not seen within it;
only when the wise skillfully smelt and refine it does the true gold finally manifest.
Even when all material forms are analyzed down to the ultimate atom, [the nature of reality remains hidden].
Furthermore, when one analyzes and seeks the various aggregates, whether as identical or distinct in nature, the essence of the Buddha cannot be seen; yet it is not that the Buddha does not exist.
When a practitioner of meditative concentration contemplates the Tathāgata, they perceive the thirty-two marks of excellence.
All various matters, such as suffering and pleasure, are clearly manifested through their performance;
therefore, one should not say that the Tathāgata is definitively non-existent.
There is the Buddha of Samādhi, and the Buddha of Skillfulness in Roots of Goodness.
The Victorious Buddha of All Worlds, And the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment— These five kinds of Buddhas exist; All others are merely emanations.
The Tathāgatagarbha is endowed with The thirty-two supreme marks.
Therefore, the Buddha is not non-existent; those who are concentrated can perceive him.
Transcending the three realms, throughout immeasurable Buddha-lands, the subtle and wondrous lands of the Tathāgata are filled with pure sons of the Buddha.
Concentration and wisdom mutually support one another, thereby forming a firm and stable nature;
they roam through the realm of Ghanavyūha, contemplating the majesty and virtue of the Buddha.
Those within Ghanavyūha all possess features identical to those of the Buddha.
Transcending momentary destruction, you constantly dwell in samādhi.
O Bhagavān, supreme within meditative concentration, adorned with all the marks,
you have attained the vision of dreams and thus manifest all phenomena.
The multitude says that the Buddha’s transformation body descends from Tuṣita;
yet the Buddha always dwells in the Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja), and it is from that realm that his images appear.
Abiding in reality and in meditative absorption, he gives rise to various manifestations according to conditions.
Just as the moon in the sky reflects its image in all waters,
And as the manifold reflections of a mani jewel appear clearly through the union of colors,
So too does the Tathāgata, abiding in right concentration, manifest his reflections in this same way.
Just as a form and its reflection are neither identical nor different, so too does the Supreme Being accomplish all his activities.
He is not composed of atoms or a primal nature; he is not Time, nor is he Īśvara.
Nor do other conditions and so forth create the world; rather,
the Tathāgata, by means of causes and conditions, adorns the essence of its fruit,
manifesting all its various forms clearly according to what is appropriate for the world.
Sporting in samādhi, there is nothing internal or external that he does not manifest.
Mountains, rivers, forests, and wilds; friends and all kinsmen;
the myriad stars, the sun, and the moon—all appear as clear reflections suspended before him.
Thus all these worlds, he completely encompasses within his body;
then placing them within the palm of his hand, he scatters and hurls them like mustard seeds.
The Buddha is sovereign in meditative concentration; the Muni is the most supreme Honored One.
There is no creator of the world; it is solely transformed by the Buddha.
Those who are foolish, obscured, and lacking wisdom are bound by the delusions of evil perceptions;
they cling to views of existence and non-existence, and perceive both self and non-self.
Some say he destroys everything, while others say it is only a small portion;
such people as these constantly bring harm upon themselves.
The Buddha pervades the three realms of existence; he is the Great Teacher of contemplative practice.
One observes the world as like a city of the gandharvas; all the various activities performed are also like forms in a dream.
Like a thirsty deer perceiving a mirage, the actions of bending and stretching are like the forward and backward movement of a puppet on a wind-driven string.
The Buddha, through his wisdom of skillful means, possesses sovereign knowledge and vision;
he is like a master craftsman who skillfully guards the mechanism of a loom,
and like a sea captain who grips the rudder and steers the ship.
Boundless, most tranquil, and sublime, It is fully possessed by the Supreme Person.
Those of sharp faculties can realize it, While those of dull faculties remain far removed from it.
This is for the practitioner of concentration, The very foundation of wondrous meditative absorption.
All those established in meditative concentration and wisdom, Dwell with clear understanding within the mind.
The Buddha-body is most pure; It is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is far removed from the duality of subject and object, And transcends the reach of the sense faculties and their measures.
The mind associated with wondrous wisdom is the supreme realm;
while all marks are the objects of delusion, the Tathāgata is free from marks.
Capable of severing all afflictions, he remains unstained within meditative concentration.
Neither moving nor moved, you abide on the path free from defilement.
Together with the subtle and wondrous devas, the gandharvas, asuras, and others,
as well as the various sages and non-Buddhists, they offer praise and constant offerings.
He is not startled or amazed by them; his mind remains unshaken.
Because of the primordial purity of yoga, he has thus transcended to the other shore.
Through the manifestations of the nirmāṇakāya buddha, he acts for the sake of gods and humans as well.
The Buddha does not manifest as this or that, just like the sun and the moon;
abiding in the wisdom of perfect responsiveness, he appears among humanity free from desire.
Toward the various non-Buddhist outsiders, he subdues them all according to what is appropriate.
The various kinds of knowledge and dharmas, the treatises on kingship and the four Vedas—
all these are maintained and expounded by the Tathāgatas through the power of meditative concentration.
They manifest in royal courts and assemblies, as well as the laws and regulations of various nations.
The mountain forests and places for practicing the Way are all manifested through the Buddha’s transformations.
The treasuries of myriad jewels in the ten directions, which produce pure and refined gems,
are all due to the sovereign majestic power of the God among Gods.
The skillful wisdom regarding the three realms, the various kinds of intellectual talents,
and the karmic activities of expedient means— all are accomplished because of the Buddha.
Holding garlands for the sake of all beings, he reveals the causes for those who practice karma.
Skilled in various forms of playful merriment, they constantly discourse on songs and verses;
sometimes manifesting their descent from Tuṣita, surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens,
they engage in song and dance with mutual joy, gathering together day and night.
Sometimes he manifests as a Mara-king, his head adorned with a jeweled crown;
wielding the cords of the world, he bestows or takes away, and summons or releases.
Though he releases all beings, he manifests as one of clear wisdom.
Always dwelling within the Ghanavyūha, it is tranquil and without movement.
This is the realm of the Great Muni, yet the ignorant and foolish engage in false conceptualization;
they are like those with cataracts in their eyes, or like deer perceiving a mirage.
Just as one perceives illusions in the world, or all that is grasped within a dream,
so too is the realm of the God among Gods; the sons of the Buddha are fully endowed with reality because they perceive its excellence, just like awakening from a dream.
Nārāyaṇa, Īśvara, Brahmā, Śana, Candra, and Mānasa,
as well as Kumāra, Kapila, and Śuka— contemplate these as well;
for if one is distracted by their spheres, one will not perceive true yoga.
The ascetic sages of the future, as well as those of the past and present,
because their minds are shrouded by habitual tendencies, are likewise unable to comprehend it.
Excellent, Vajragarbha!
Having traversed all the stages through universal practice, and further by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, he dwells in the Land of Secret Adornment.
This Vajragarbha manifests entry into meditative absorption;
this is the realm of those in right concentration, because of his union with it.
Some may falsely discriminate, [claiming] that there is a Primal Nature (prakṛti) or atoms (paramāṇu),
like a craftsman fashioning objects with their various distinct characteristics.
But arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and ceasing is likewise merely the ceasing of dharmas.
One falsely conceives that all things are produced by subtle atoms;
yet, just as a lamp reveals objects, so too does a cause allow for the cognition of its effect.
From the beginning, no characteristic can be apprehended, and the same is true when it later perishes.
Within the past, no intrinsic entity can be found;
the future is likewise so. Apart from conditions, there is no inherent nature.
Within each and every condition, though sought everywhere, no entity exists.
They also perceive the nature of existence and non-existence, yet they lack even the view of non-existence.
They conceptualize a subtle self, sentient beings, jars, garments, and the like;
these heterodox schools destroy the right path—there are three hundred and sixty such views.
“Coming and going within birth and death, there is no dharma of nirvāṇa. **Chapter Two:

Entering the Subtle and Wondrous Body of Ghanavyūha (Part One)** *The Mahāyāna Ghanavyūha Sūtra: Chapter Two, Entering the Subtle and Wondrous Body of Ghanavyūha* At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvabuddhadharmatathatādarśana, whose body was adorned with necklaces of jewels and who possessed immeasurable power and sovereignty in the world, rose from his seat. Placing his right knee upon the ground, he addressed Vajragarbha in these words:

“Venerable One, you have thoroughly mastered the three vehicles of the world; your mind is free from contradiction, and you possess the wisdom of internal realization dwelling in happiness in the present life. As a great master of meditative concentration, you are sovereign over samādhi and can explain the characteristics of the various stages in accordance with reality. You constantly abide within all buddha-fields, acting as a leader for all to expound the profound and wondrous Dharma.”

Therefore, I now exhort the sons of the Buddha to explain the realm of internal realization—the state of dwelling in happiness in the present life—which is not dependent on others and belongs to the noble ones.

Now that I and the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have seen this Dharma, we shall practice with ease and advance toward the stage of Buddhahood. We shall obtain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and the body of speech, becoming fully endowed with sovereign power and supernormal faculties. We shall transform our basis of existence (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) yet not abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Like a *cintāmaṇi* gem of many colors, manifesting all forms and images, we shall be able to expound the practices of the *Ghanavyūha* within the palaces of the heavenly kings across all realms of rebirth, as well as within the Ghanavyūha realm of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
“Excellent, O Lord of Gods and Men, Most eminent among Bodhisattvas!
Please explain the entry into the Guhyasamāja, The dharma-nature of non-self.”
One should realize that the objects of discrimination are the signs grasped by the mind.
If one abandons discrimination, one will see the world as mere discrimination;
by thoroughly understanding the objective referents of the world, one attains samādhi.
I shall now expound this for you; O Lord of Men, listen attentively.
When one sees a mirage in the heat, the characteristics of the world are likewise so;
though there are causes for the characteristic and the characterized, there is no false conceptualization.
The cognizer can arise from the cognized, and the cognized appears in dependence upon the cognizer;
apart from those, this does not exist, like light and shadow following one another.
When there is no mind, there is also no object; both the subject and the object of cognition are absent.
Relying solely upon the single mind, one thus makes such distinctions.
Both the knowing subject and the known object are merely what exists within the measure of the mind;
since the known mind is absent, the knower cannot be found.
The mind is the intrinsic nature of phenomena; when its inherent nature is disturbed and turbid, it becomes purified at the eighth stage.
At the ninth stage, one attains meditative absorption;
with awakened wisdom as the tenth stage, one receives empowerment and realizes the state of a Tathāgata.
The Dharma-body attains inexhaustibility; this is the realm of the Buddha.
Ultimately like empty space, the mind and consciousness are likewise so:
inexhaustible and indestructible, adorned with all virtues.
Ever abiding in the inconceivable, the secret and majestic realm of all Buddhas.
Just as when a jar is broken, the nature of the shards becomes manifest;
when the shards are broken, the fine dust appears; and when the dust is analyzed, the ultimate atom is revealed.
Thus, by means of conditioned causes, one accomplishes the untainted dharmas.
Just as when fire has consumed the fuel and continues to burn elsewhere, so too upon realizing suchness,
one attains the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) and becomes far removed from conceptual construction.
Abiding in immovable wisdom, they manifest within the Guhyasamāja.
Though unborn, they appear in manifold forms; dwelling in no world, they sever all views—take refuge in this selflessness.
The continuous flow is severed; there is neither destruction nor arising.
One who can exhaust all views takes refuge in this selflessness.
All afflictions have been extinguished; it is tranquil and inconceivable.
It can purify all views; take refuge in this selflessness.
The various phenomena of the world are, from the beginning, devoid of a self-nature.
They do not become non-existent through being struck or destroyed, but are revealed as such by means of metaphors.
Just as fire, having consumed its fuel, is extinguished of its own accord within it,
so too is the wisdom that perceives the three realms of existence as selfless;
this is called the bliss of the present life, the sphere of internal realization.
By relying on this, one enters the various stages, purifying the evils of beginningless time;
abandoning worldly dependencies, one dwells in the supramundane.
As the mind becomes ever more purified, one constantly abides in the Land of Secret Adornment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Yathābhūta-darśin, along with the various kings and others, addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"We all now wish to take refuge; we pray only that you will show us the place of refuge."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha replied in verse:
“The Buddha-body is neither existent nor non-existent; Having already incinerated the tree of the aggregates, He transcends the hosts of Māra And dwells in the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha).”
Awakened, pure, and stainless— O Lord of Men, you are worthy of refuge.
Transcending the measure of cognition and realizing the state of non-existence—
O Lord of Men, you who dwell in the *Ghanavyūha* samādhi, you are worthy of refuge.
The Pure and Exalted Ghanavyūha realm, The dwelling place relied upon by all the sages,
Filled with practitioners of contemplation— One should take refuge in Ghanavyūha.
One should contemplate the world As being like a landscape of high and low that has come to an end.
Seeing beautiful forms in a dream, A barren woman suddenly giving birth—
These are like the city of Gandharvas, Like a fire-wheel or hair in the sky,
Like various illusory forms, And like people, horses, flowers, fruits, and trees.
That which returns to its illusory transformations is entirely without reality.
Like rushing lightning or floating clouds, all things are merely provisional and not substantial;
like a craftsman fashioning a jar, they are produced through conceptual construction.

O Benevolent Lord, you should listen attentively: all sentient beings in the world have their minds constantly shrouded by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), giving rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
The *manas*, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the continuity of the remaining consciousnesses [function in this way].
The five dharmas and the three natures, And the two kinds of selflessness, are ever in constant association.
Just as when the wind strikes violent waters, Various waves of consciousness arise; As the waves are born, the flow never ceases.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise: the various habitual tendencies from beginningless time are like those turbulent waters;
moved by the winds of objects, the waves of the various consciousnesses arise, never ceasing for even a moment.
The eight kinds of flowing mind, though lacking any manifold substance,
may arise suddenly according to conditions or may be produced gradually;
their apprehension of objects is likewise characterized by such distinctions between the gradual and the sudden.
The mind transforms into houses, the sun, moon, and constellations,
the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of trees, as well as mountain forests and military hosts;
within such places as these, it can arise both gradually and instantaneously.
For the most part, these can manifest simultaneously, or arise gradually with distinctions.
When, within a dream, one perceives objects previously experienced,
as well as the initial arising of thoughts and conceptions, up to old age and death—
Calculating numbers and various objects, investigating the meanings of phrases,
observing diverse literary styles, and partaking of fine foods—
within such spheres of experience, one is gradually able to attain full understanding.
At times it arises suddenly, yet there is one who can grasp it.
The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and inconceivable;
it is the wondrous treasury of the Tathāgata, like gold existing within ore.
The mind-born arises from the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the other six are likewise so.
The six types of consciousness, or more, are differentiated within the three realms;
they consist of the ālaya, the perfuming agents (vāsanās), and the remaining mental factors (caitta-dharmas).
The seeds of defilement and purity, though dwelling together, remain untainted;
the Buddha-lineage is likewise: it is neither fixed nor eternally pure.
It is like the ocean water which remains constant, yet its waves and tides shift and flow.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise: according to the distinctions of the stages, its cultivation has lower, middle, and upper levels; by abandoning defilement, it becomes manifest.
Vajragarbha spoke again:
“O Bodhisattva Yathābhūta-darśin!
Those who see, hear, perceive, and awaken possess the wisdom of the suchness of intrinsic nature.
Throughout all lands in the ten directions, amidst the assemblies of all kings—”
You have already heard this from me; explain it extensively as appropriate.
If a person, having heard the Dharma, gradually purifies the ālayavijñāna, they may become a king among men, a wheel-turning monarch over the four continents.
Or again, they become Śakra, or dwell in Tuṣita, Suyāma, and so forth,
even up to the palace of Nirmāṇarati, as sovereign lords of the desire realm;
or they reign over the abodes of the form realm, or are born among the gods of the formless realm.
Among the non-conceptual beings, they experience the bliss of meditative concentration;
realizing the truth, they do not abide therein. Like the roar of a lion, they possess mastery over all samādhis and are in harmony with the joy of the Dharma.
Single-mindedly seeking the Ghanavyūha, one remains unstained by the three realms.
Having reached the Ghanavyūha, one gradually awakens;
through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), one attains peace and bliss, dwelling eternally in tranquility.
Surrounded by and adorned with immeasurable sons of the Buddha,
he is the sovereign king of the Dharma, the most supreme among the assembly.
It is not as the non-Buddhists claim— that nirvana consists in annihilation.
If it were subject to destruction, it would be identical to conditioned phenomena; furthermore, there would be the fault of [the self] being born again.
The ten karmas—superior, middling, and inferior—are the source from which the three vehicles arise.
From the most superior, one is born into the Guhyavajra Realm (Ghanavyūha), ascending and progressing through each successive stage.
Having attained the wisdom of liberation and the subtle, wondrous body of a Tathāgata,
why do you speak of nirvāṇa as a phenomenon subject to disintegration?
If nirvāṇa were subject to disintegration, sentient beings would have an end.
If sentient beings had an end, they would likewise have a beginning;
there would have to be something that is not a "sentient being" that first becomes one,
for there is nothing that is not a sentient being that arises within the realm of sentient beings.
If the realm of sentient beings were exhausted, there would be no dharma for a Buddha to know;
thus, there would be no one capable of awakening, nor would there be nirvāṇa.
Those who falsely conceptualize liberation merely speak of liberation.
Like a lamp extinguished when the fuel is spent, or like the core of a plantain tree;
he who realizes the nature of liberation destroys existence to achieve non-existence.
Regarding the sublime bliss of liberation, one who remains detached cannot describe it.
In the spheres of totality and the meditative absorptions, in the formless attainments and the attainment of non-perception,
entering and emerging from them in both forward and reverse order— with power and supernormal faculties all mastered,
he does not regress therein, nor does he ever remain submerged.
Thoroughly comprehending the characteristics of phenomena, Attaining skillfulness in the various stages (*bhūmi*),
And thus adorning oneself, one shall go To the future realm of Ghanavyūha.
If one says that the nature of liberation Destroys existence to establish non-existence,
Such a person dwells within the various realms of existence and is ultimately unable to escape.
Having destroyed the threefold conjunction— the four types of conditions such as causes,
as well as the internal and external conditions of the eye and form— the consciousness produced by their conjunction [is likewise destroyed].
The internal and external phenomena of the world arise through mutual influence;
all such manifold meanings are entirely subverted [by this].
If one knows that these are manifestations of consciousness-only, they are seen to be apart from what is apprehended by the mind.
When conceptualization does not manifest, one likewise does not abide in its nature.
At that time, being free from objects of perception, the mind enters a state of tranquil meditative absorption (samāpatti).
Having abandoned the world, one relinquishes the views of the grasped and the grasper.
Through the transformation of the basis, one is freed from coarse heaviness;
With inconceivable wisdom and the ten kinds of mind-made bodies, Adorned with all manner of wonders,
acting as the sovereign of the three realms, One is born in the Ghanavyūha.
Form, mind, and mental factors, along with their associated states and unconditioned phenomena—
whether internal, external, or worldly— if one observes them with discernment as being without distinction,
such wise ones shall come to the Land of Secret Adornment.
Names, signs, and conceptualization, correct wisdom and suchness— these,
along with the samādhis of the Muni, are equal in their essential nature.
One should go to the Guhyasamāja, the land praised by the Buddha.
If one destroys the threefold conjunction and the four types of conditions,
one does not remain firm in one's own school and becomes like those who engage in false conceptualization.
For those with evil habitual tendencies toward conceptualization, their fivefold treatises—
The analogies are not established, and all meanings are mutually contradictory.
Those five all result in fallacies, confusing the eye of awakened wisdom;
through attachment to analogies and pseudo-analogies, one falls into the error of regarding the inverted as non-inverted.
Thus, through such false attachments, everything here is destroyed;
abandoning one's own doctrine and relying on the tenets of others,
all views regarding the beginningless past and so forth arise from this destruction.
Great King, you should know that sentient beings within the three realms revolve like a wheel; their beginning cannot be found.
Out of compassionate vows, the Tathāgata universally responds to all who have a karmic connection.
Like the radiance of the pure moon, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
According to the nature of their prior karma, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities.
If he were to destroy nirvāṇa, what benefit or merit would the Buddha have?
There are three kinds of higher training, and liberation is likewise;
the Four Truths and the bases of psychic power, the foundations of mindfulness and the analytical knowledges,
the four conditions and the immaterial abodes, the faculties, the powers, and the supernormal knowledges.
The factors of enlightenment, the various stages, and so forth, Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,
even up to the noble sages, All exist in dependence upon consciousness.
The patience regarding the dharma of suffering and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, The subsequent patience regarding suffering and the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
The same applies to the knowledge of origination; the knowledges of cessation and the path are likewise so.
These sixteen types are called "clear realization" (abhisamaya).
There are ten types of persons in training (śaikṣa); the eighth is one who has seven more births remaining.
One who goes from family to family, one who returns only once more, and one who attains extinction in the interval;
those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, those who attain it with effort, and those who attain it without effort;
those who go upstream to various realms—only after these do they enter parinirvāṇa.
In all these various modes, the stages and categories of all wisdoms differ as inferior,
middling, or superior for those who practice contemplation;
yet the superior cultivation of the Bodhisattvas is the most preeminent in merit.
The eleventh and the twelfth, as well as the sixteenth—
these practitioners of meditative concentration further gradually extinguish the mind;
that which is exhausted is not the mind, nor does it coexist with the mind.
The future mind has not yet arrived; because it has not arrived, it does not exist.
When the conditions for the mind are not in harmony, it is neither produced from this nor from that.
In the fourth dhyāna there is no mind, yet its causes cannot destroy it.
There is a cause, namely the various consciousnesses—the mental consciousness and the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
Through deluded conceptualization, they do not realize this; they flow and turn like waves.
One who is established in meditative concentration observes the ālayavijñāna, free from the discrimination of subject and object.
Subtle and non-existent, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is indestructible;
dwelling in the Buddha-field of Ghanavyūha, they manifest like the lunar disc.
The wise ones of Ghanavyūha are always in the company of the Buddhas.
Constantly wandering within the realm of meditative concentration, there is a single flavor without distinction.
This inconceivable sphere of contemplative practice is born from the power of meditative stability;
Your Majesty should constantly cultivate it, remaining in accord with this subtle and wondrous samādhi.
In the six heavens of the desire realm, and again in the twelve Brahma realms,
as well as in the formless and non-conceptual states— among all these stages,
if one is born in the Land of Secret Adornment, one shall become a lord of gods therein.
Those who seek the Land of Secret Adornment Should cultivate the ten kinds of knowledge:
The knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge, Knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge, The knowledge of suffering,
its origin, cessation, and the path, As well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
O Benevolent Lord, those born of your lineage— Śāṇakavṛddha,
the Moon King, and Ikṣvāku— are equal in their noble descent;
yet even among those clans, yours is the most preeminent.
One should seek the Land of Secret Adornment, Do not harbor doubt or a regressive mind;
Like a sheep being led by a rope, Panting with fear, it retreats.
The manas within the body Abides like a phantom deer.
They are like the shadow of a magical tree, or reeds and rushes in a river.
Like a king sporting in a garden, moving his limbs,
so too are the mind and the mental consciousness, together with all mental factors, arising in conjunction.
This dharma has no intrinsic nature, Like a mass of clouds that is not real.
The storehouse consciousness with all its seeds Is shrouded and covered by habitual tendencies;
Just like that mani jewel, It manifests various colors according to conditions.
Though dwelling within the bodies of sentient beings, it is like a stainless king of swans;
this is the definitive lineage, and it is also Great Nirvana.
Names arise from signs, and signs arise from causes and conditions.
Due to various forms and characteristics, conceptual discrimination arises.
This discrimination arises from two causes: external perceptions and the habitual tendencies of the mind;
it should be known that the seventh consciousness, manas, is likewise so.
When the sense faculties, the mind, and their objects converge, the five consciousnesses arise;
conjoined with mental factors, they dwell within the body like inhabitants in a palace.
The King of Wisdom constantly observes all the worlds.
From such causes as these, those various fruits arise;
True Suchness is not different from this, for all phenomena are mutually produced.
With a mind that accords with principle, one can clearly perceive and contemplate this.
This is precisely the nature of all phenomena, the ultimate perfected nature;
yet it is also that which is falsely conceptualized as "all phenomena are unarisen.
The nature of all phenomena is eternally empty; it is neither non-existent nor existent.
Like an illusion and like a dream, As well as a city of Gandharvas,
a mirage, and the floating hair-tufts, Like smoke, clouds, and other such things—
These various forms and characteristics, And the collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
When such attachment arises, the nature of pervasive imagination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is established.
Through the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and the mind, habitual perfuming (vāsanā) forms seeds;
these are not distinct from the mind, and all consciousnesses arise from them.
Relying on the power of mutual causation, this is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Having perfectly realized the wisdom of self-awakening, manifesting in the dwelling of the bliss of the Dharma—
this is explained as the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), the realm of all the noble ones.
The Buddha and his sons have realized this and are thus called noble ones (*ārya*).
If a person realizes this Dharma, they immediately behold the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and proclaim:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established."
There is nothing that he does not accomplish; he no longer undergoes future existence.
He is liberated from all suffering and has severed all agitation.
Having burned away all habitual tendencies, he remains unshakable even at the end of an eon.
Having realized that both the person and phenomena are without self, he clearly perceives them all as empty.
All the various conceptual proliferations accumulated since beginningless time,
along with their boundless faults and afflictions— all have been completely eliminated.
Just as when a ball of hot iron cools, the heat departs while the iron remains unimpaired,
so too the one who is liberated, with afflictions exhausted,
attains coolness and enters the untainted realm, the wondrous land of Ghanavyūha.
This land is most subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of others;
it is the dwelling place of purity for only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
With samādhi manifest before them, they take this as their sustenance.
Those who wish to be born in this land should skillfully practice sublime yoga;
furthermore, for the sake of all those with whom they have a karmic connection, they should analyze and extensively reveal it.
Names arise from characteristics, and characteristics, in turn, arise from conditions.
From the conceptualization of arising from causes and conditions, one does not accord with the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Roots, objects, jars, garments, and so forth—these are conventional phenomena that arise through mutual conjunction;
from these, conceptualization is born, which perceives them as distinct and separate.
Whether moving or unmoving, all worlds arise from the darkness of delusion;
their very substance is ignorant obscurity.
Short and long forms, as well as sounds and the realm of fragrances—
Taste, bitterness, hardness, smoothness, and so forth, are the objects of perception for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). All phenomena— whether wholesome or unwholesome,
conditioned or unconditioned, even up to nirvāṇa— are the domain of wisdom.
Moment by moment they are constantly shifting and transforming, all arising because of consciousness.
The manas takes the ālayavijñāna as its object, like a magnet attracting iron;
it is like a snake with two heads, each separately performing its own function.
The defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is likewise: grasping the *ālayavijñāna*, it performs the functions of a self;
it increases the sense of "mine" (*mamakāra*), and further, in conjunction with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it transforms and passes away as its cause.
Warmth arises within the body; it moves and performs various actions.
Food, drink, and clothing are enjoyed according to their nature.
One leaps and bounds, or engages in song and dance, sporting in various ways for one's own amusement.
The bodies sustained by all sentient beings arise entirely through the power of the mind.
Like a whirling firebrand or falling hair, or like the city of the gandharvas, they are not understood to be nothing but one's own mind;
thus, false conceptualizations are erroneously produced.
The physical body, its marks, and the vessel-world are like the motion of a swing;
lacking power and devoid of solidity, conceptualization is likewise.
Conceptualization has no basis; it functions solely within its own domain.
Just as an image in a mirror appears when the seeds of consciousness stir, so too do fools become deluded; this is not the case for those of clear wisdom.
O Lord of Men, you should know that these three are all manifestations of consciousness.
In this place of seclusion, this is the perfectly accomplished reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Bodhisattvas such as Dhṛtiprabha and others, as well as the noble Maudgalyāyana,
sought by sound and surveyed everywhere across hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lands.
Adorned with various jewels, its splendor is peerless;
among those subtle and wondrous realms, Ghanavyūha is most excellent.
So too are the lands of Sukhāvatī and Abhirati, and the billions of worlds below.
All the World-Honored Ones praise such a land as this,
saying it has neither beginning nor end, and its majestic virtue transforms spontaneously.
It is the dwelling place of Buddhas of the past, transcending the three realms.
Abundant joy is not grasped; in tranquility, one is spontaneously unconditioned.
Having perfected both self-benefit and the benefit of others, all meritorious deeds are fully accomplished.
Without remaining within the realm of desire, one attains Buddhahood and performs the Buddha-work.
Desiring to go to the Land of Secret Adornment to realize unsurpassed enlightenment,
the koṭis of World-Honored Ones who wish to perform Buddha-works within the realm of desire first emanate from this land in immeasurable billions of forms.
Constantly in accord with right concentration, they sport with supernormal powers throughout all lands; like the moon, there is nowhere they are not seen,
benefiting and transforming all classes of sentient beings according to their needs.
The *Daśabhūmika*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and others, the *Mahāvaipulya* and the *Abhijñā*,
the *Śrīmālā* and other sūtras— all emerge from this sūtra. Thus,
the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* is the most excellent among all sūtras.
The benevolent lord and all other kings should offer their utmost respect.
The Tathāgata has long since transcended the realms of desire, form, and formlessness,
as well as the celestial palaces of the Non-conceptualizing Heaven and others, yet he dwells in the Secret Adornment.
The various palaces of this land, adorned like lotuses,
are the sublime manifestations of the pure wisdom of all Tathāgatas;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas always abide within them.
The World-Honored One constantly dwells in dhyāna, Tranquility supreme and unsurpassed;
Relying on his own inconceivable samādhi, He manifests a multitude of wondrous forms.
These manifestations of form are boundless, And cannot be seen by others.
In the Land of Utmost Bliss, adorned with splendor, The World-Honored One Amitāyus—
the physical forms of all those who practice contemplation are likewise of such appearance.
Some see the God among Gods, resplendent and imbued with myriad colors.
The color of the female *campaka* flower, the luster of pure gold and the bright moon;
like the neck of a peacock or a lotus, a cluster of *śirīṣa* seeds;
the colors of a rainbow, lightning, and coral; or appearing in a body that is pure and emaciated.
Some wear robes of kusha grass, or sleep upon beds of straw and thatch;
some dwell upon lotus flowers, radiant like the light of a thousand suns.
Some see various bodhisattvas, their heads adorned with topknots of coiled dragons.
A diamond and sapphire-blue jewel, Adorned as a precious crown;
Or one may see the marks of wheels and banners, Or the signs of fish, conchs, and so forth;
Or one may see a radiant and beautiful color, Like a rainbow trailing across the sky.
Or taking Mount Sumeru, he places it within the palm of his hand;
or holding the waters of the great ocean, he settles them within the print of a cow’s hoof;
or he manifests as a king of men, wearing the ceremonial crown and robes while standing in the hall of his palace.
His attendants all show reverence, together proclaiming the transformation of the nation;
some appear in the field of Ghanavyūha, those who practice meditation in tranquility,
expounding the realm of self-realization and the dharmas known by the luminous Buddhas.
Some say they have attained the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), with both mind and wisdom liberated,
possessing mastery over samādhi and an unimpeded body like an illusion;
others manifest objects without being stained by them, severing all karma of grasping and attachment.
With wisdom he burns the fuel of views, and no longer undergoes the various realms of existence.
Like a lamp whose oil and wick are exhausted, it is extinguished and enters nirvana;
yet sometimes he manifests the cultivation of the perfections, holding great assemblies where he bestows gifts without restriction.
Through the observance of precepts, ascetic practices, and various ritual regulations, one is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, adorned with splendor. There, beings are not born from a womb;
they possess subtle, golden bodies, radiant, pure, and perfect.
The realms of those multitudes are all fully endowed with yoga;
yet compared to the Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha), they do not equal even one hundredth part of it.
Those in the realm of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) naturally obtain food according to their thoughts.
The Muni, supreme and sovereign, has attained the nectar-like flavor of meditative concentration;
beneath various jewel-tree groves where he wanders and rests,
the ground is strewn with golden sand, manifesting a most excellent realm.
Pure and wondrous jewel lotuses, blooming with the waters of merit—
such a sublime realm is beyond all comparison.
All those born from the lotuses pay homage to Amitāyus.
Those who have well cultivated samādhi, who delight in the virtues of the Buddha,
and who single-mindedly dedicate their merit, shall all be born in that land;
adorned with the various marks, they will be as clear and mirror-like as they are free from dust and defilement.
When Vajragarbha had finished speaking, he manifested within his own body:
sometimes like a finger joint, or again like a mustard seed,
or as fine as the tip of a hair, even a hundredth part of that.
Sometimes manifesting the body of a Sugata, or as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
in various forms and other categories, even in all manner of shapes,
he teaches the various dharmas according to what is appropriate for each.
Or it is said that for a bodhisattva, having entered the various stages and realized the five dharmas,
the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness,
they attain the illusion-like samādhi and manifest bodies according to their will.
Mastery over all supernormal powers, the ten strengths, and the four fearlessnesses;
abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, having attained the pure basis of reliance,
entering into the ground of the Buddhas, and the untainted aggregates and elements.
Forever free from all other transformations, He abides eternally in tranquil stillness.
Or it is said that for the Bodhisattva, who wanders with skillful grace,
it is like a dream, a reflection, or the moon in water— the path traversed by the yogin.
Having attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, With ten kinds of illusion-like bodies and ten inexhaustible vows fulfilled, He realizes Equal and Perfect Enlightenment;
Seated upon a wondrous lotus throne, His marks and signs are exceedingly dignified and majestic.
Immeasurable sons of the Buddhas respectfully surround them.
Some speak of how bodhisattvas, through the power of their vows, manifest various forms,
traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions and serving Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These bodhisattvas possess bodies of extreme subtlety;
they always enter and emerge with mastery, dwelling neither in existence nor non-existence.
They are like celestial seers and gandharvas.
Dwelling upon that Mount Sumeru, or abiding in the void,
they are not seen by the sentient beings who travel upon the earth;
likewise, the manifestation of these Bodhisattvas is also thus.
Except for those who practice meditative contemplation, no one is able to behold them.
Some say that the various bodhisattvas, having attained supreme dhyāna,
manifest births in all places and demonstrate entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder.
It is said that some Bodhisattvas, by means of their power of meditative concentration,
are able to freely transform their basis; without dwelling in the limit of reality,
they manifest various distinct bodies throughout the realms of immeasurable sentient beings.
Though their bodies are of various kinds, their minds are one and equal,
just like the earth and water, and also like the sun and moon.
Some say that all bodhisattvas always possess a mind of great compassion.

Sentient and insentient beings, as well as all phenomena, whether moving or unmoving—[all are thus].
All are like jars and such, having the nature of disintegration and destruction.
Lord of Devas, you should know that all consciousnesses are extremely subtle, shifting and flowing with great speed; this is the domain of the Buddhas.
Various seers and non-Buddhists falsely claim to be Muni;
bound by their words to one another, they crave all manner of forms.
Regarding this arising and ceasing consciousness, they are entirely unable to know it.

Or, whatever fruit may be obtained through four months of asceticism or through sacrificial offerings—

Bound by the fruits of the three qualities, one is as unsubstantial as a plantain tree;
only through liberation by means of wisdom can one be born in the Ghanavyūha realm.
Only when a practitioner realizes this state can they proceed to that palace.
Therefore, Great Brahmā, you should practice this well.
Those within the Guhyasamāja have no kinship with birth and death;
all their sentient consciousnesses are neither interrupted nor destroyed.
All karmas are free from attachment, And likewise free from the perfuming of defilements;
Like a lotus unsoiled by water, Or like space untainted by dust,
The sun and moon are free from the veil of clouds— So too is the practitioner of yoga.
Swiftly cultivate this contemplative practice, sustained by the Tathāgata;
bathe in the stream of pure precepts and drink the essence of wisdom.
Through the cultivation of sublime morality and wisdom, one attains liberation from birth and death.
O Lord of Devas, you should know that the aggregates, bases,
and elements of sentient beings are composed of a multitude of dharmas, all of which are utterly non-existent.
Through the causal conditions of the eye, forms, and so forth, consciousness arises.
Just as fire blazes because of fuel, so too does consciousness arise.
Objects revolve following the deluded mind, like iron drawn toward a magnet;
they are like a city of Gandharvas or a mirage, grasped by the ignorant who thirst.
Within, there is no creator; it is merely the transformation following the mind.
Furthermore, like those in a city of *gandharvas*, their coming and going are entirely unreal.
The bodies of sentient beings are likewise; their every movement and stillness is not truly real.
Just as one sees things within a dream, which no longer exist upon waking,
so too the falsely perceived phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are fundamentally quiescent once one has awakened.
The multitude of atoms of the four great elements cannot be found apart from the mind.
Among all things in the world that can be grasped, which is not composed of the four great elements?
Just as when the condition of a wind-disorder arises, various objects may appear to the sight, yet the reanimated corpse has no agent; so too it is with the phenomena of the world.
You, sons of the Buddhas, should carefully observe that all moving and stationary things in the world are like a mass of foam;
like the false imaginings of jars, garments, and the like, they are as unreal as a mirage.
All sensations, such as suffering and pleasure, are like bubbles upon the water;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like the plantain tree, lacking any solid core within.
This consciousness is like a magical illusion; it is deceptive and entirely unreal.
Within those three realms, all phenomena— whether moving or unmoving—
are identical to dream-visions; they are manifestations of the deluded mind,
like illusory transformations and the city of the gandharvas.
It merely deceives the foolish; from the beginning, it possesses no reality.
When a Son of the Buddha awakens to this dharma, his mind is free from fear.
The fire of wisdom incinerates all afflictions, and he is immediately born in the Land of Secret Adornment.
The world is entirely without marks; it is by marks that one is bound.
To be without marks is auspicious. Marks and the sphere of the mind—the sphere of the mind is not real; reality is the sphere of wisdom.
Far removed from all signs, it is the practice of compassion;
signless and pervasive throughout all things, the three realms are entirely pure.
The various signs such as form and sound are called the phenomena of the three realms.
All sense faculties and their objects are the causes that bind sentient beings;
through wisdom one attains liberation, dwelling in peace and sovereignty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin sat upon an exquisite throne.

having accomplished the most sublime wisdom, you have thoroughly realized all knowable phenomena.”
Regarding the immeasurable *siddhāntas*, he has already attained clear vision of them all.

he observes the bodies of sentient beings and the fundamental arising of all things.
Expounded with wondrous sounds, they could not be exhausted even throughout kalpas.

May these wise ones, with minds pure and free from doubt,

Wisdom can liberate one from suffering, while sensation constitutes a firm bondage.
Arising from the minds of sentient beings, through form, light, mental attention,
and other such conditions, it scatters and wanders among various objects.

by ignorance, craving, and karma, it is clouded and disturbed.
All phenomena are preceded by the mind; the mind is swift, and the mind is supreme.
Phenomena correspond with the mind; all take the mind as their nature.

Just as a mani jewel of many colors manifests according to those colors,

possessing the image of the Tathāgata, he dwells eternally in the palace of mastery.

The wondrous land upon which all practitioners of contemplation rely is neither interrupted nor an object; it is eternally abiding and immutable.

The thesis and all its constituent parts are entirely of an indeterminate nature.
Because they each cling to differences regarding tenets and reasons,

the subtle realm of Ghanavyūha— whose essence is the consciousness of the transformed basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and which transcends the discriminating mind— is not an object of deluded conceptualization.
The Tathāgata’s Land of Secret Adornment has neither end nor beginning;
it is not of the nature of subtle atoms, nor is it produced by desire,
nor created by Maheśvara, nor born of ignorance, craving, or karma.
Arising solely from effortless, wondrous wisdom, it transcends the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and surpasses the dark net of non-conceptualization.
This is the subtle and wondrous land of Ghanavyūha; this is the *āryasiddhānta*.
It is not the domain of those who measure through logic,

Even up to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), it cannot be fully comprehended by wisdom;

Listen now attentively, O Noble One: the foolish are deluded regarding the world.
I shall now expound this meaning of karma and non-karma,

All things, both internal and external, are seen as nothing but one's own mind.

The essence of the mind has two gates; thus, the mind perceives all phenomena.
Ordinary beings are deluded in nature and cannot comprehend their own [mind].
Just as the color and form of a jar appear, they have no intrinsic nature and are only one's own mind;
yet those with weak concentration and the various seers are deluded regarding this meaning,
abandoning the principle of ultimate reality and proceeding along the path of conceptual discrimination.
This mind possesses two natures: Like a mirror reflecting the moon's image, Or like eyes affected by cataracts, One falsely perceives floating hairs.
Just as there are no floating hairs in the sky, So too should there be no pearl necklaces.
It is only from the eyes afflicted by cataracts that such things appear;
those who cling to false imaginings fail to realize this and constantly grasp at them,
seeing vast displays of various ornaments and the diverse forms of Brahmā and others.
All sentient beings, as well as jars, garments,
and other such diverse internal and external phenomena, all arise from the mind.
This sublime meditative absorption of Ghanavyūha is not possessed by others.
If there are practitioners who are born in lands of manifold merit,
or in the realm of Mastery over Desire, or among the gods of the Form Realm,
even in the palaces of the Signless and the station of Akaniṣṭha, the Highest Heaven of Form;
In the realms of emptiness, consciousness, and nothingness, and in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
within these various celestial palaces— one gradually eliminates all craving and desire;

Surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons, they sport with sovereign ease.
You should cultivate this samādhi; why do you cling to your kinsmen?
Kinsmen are a constant bondage, the very cause of wandering through birth and death.

For nine months or ten, That body gradually grows.
When the time arrived and he emerged from the womb, he was like a wriggling insect;

I observe all sentient beings: in every birth, it is exactly thus.
Parents are beyond counting, and the same is true for wives and children;
throughout all the worlds, there is nowhere they do not pervade.
It is like a barren woman who, in a dream, suddenly gives birth to a son.
Having been born, one rejoices; soon thereafter, seeing their death, one’s grief is beyond restraint.
Suddenly awakening from sleep, one no longer sees the child—neither at the moment of birth nor at the end.
Furthermore, one dreams of wandering through mountains and rivers, cities and towns,

where people see one another and hasten back and forth.
The movement of walking and the extension and contraction of limbs, as well as the immeasurable realms,
and even that which arises from waking and sleeping— all these are non-existent.
It is just like one who is full of desire seeing a woman in a dream.
His countenance was exceedingly dignified and handsome, And his garments and ornaments were all rare and exquisite;
Though he indulged in every kind of pleasure, Upon awakening, it was found that none of it remained.
One should know that all worlds Are likewise just like this.
Royal rank and its retinue, parents and kinsmen—these merely deceive the foolish; their essential nature is entirely unreal.
Why do you not diligently cultivate samādhi?
Immeasurable śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas dwell among the mountains and beneath trees in places of tranquil meditation;
