Mahendra, Kailāsa, and the Himavat mountains;
some dwell beneath the Pārijāta tree, or reside on Mount Krauñca;
some stay at the midpoint of Sumeru, or rest beneath the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
Bound by the sword-demon, one remains in silent repose therein;
partaking of the fruits of Jambudvīpa and drinking the flavor of nectar,
endowed with all supernormal powers, one constantly cultivates this contemplation.
In the past and future worlds, seated upon a lotus pedestal, he dwells in the meditative equipoise of full-lotus posture; thus he constantly observes.
Because he has well-restrained all his sense faculties, he does not scatter toward any objects.
Just as an elephant is restrained with a hook, so too is one who abides in meditative concentration.
Whether worldly or supramundane, compared to all other concentrations, the Buddha’s concentration is pure and stainless; it utterly eliminates all craving and attachment.
Pervasive attachment to the formless attainments, within the meditations such as the non-conceptual state,
seeing the forms of the sun and moon, lotuses, and deep abysses,
or various colors like fire in the sky— such false concentrations are not ultimate.
Having brushed away such signs, one attains purity and non-conceptuality;
then one sees millions of realms where the Buddhas abide in meditative equipoise,
simultaneously extending their hands to pour water over one’s crown.
They immediately enter the stage of Buddhahood, manifesting in various forms and colors.
Having attained these manifold bodies, they are endowed with omniscience (sarvajñā),
powers, supernormal faculties, and masteries, as well as right concentration and dhāraṇīs.
Such qualities as these are all fully accomplished.
By analyzing all forms down to the observation of the subtlest atom,
one finds that their intrinsic nature is non-existent, just like the horns of a rabbit.
Without parts and without conceptual differentiation, the aggregates and that which possesses aggregates are likewise;
like a magical illusion, all things are thus.
Within this, there is no karma or its fruit, nor is there any person who performs actions.
There is no agent for the world.
Even if there were an agent, since an agent depends upon an action, how could one be called an "agent"?
This statement results in a logical fallacy.
I have established all realms: the earth mandala rests upon the water mandala, as do the world of sentient beings; these are arranged in successive order.
The various destinies are each distinct, and beings pass to and fro among them.
When the faculties arise toward objects and are able to apprehend their respective domains,
these do not occur by means of a self; they are all merely conceptual constructions that undergo successive transformations, just like milk, curd, and ghee.
Thus, regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing, one calculates what is karma and what is not.
The meditative practitioner constantly contemplates these as being like a city of Gandharvas or a dream.
From beginningless time, conceptual proliferation has perfumed sentient beings.
Various faults and transgressions give rise to the karma of discrimination.
The sense faculties are like illusions, and their objects are like dreams;
the agent and the action performed can be fully distanced by one who is concentrated.
Those with weak and inferior discernment are deluded and give rise to false imaginings;
they discriminate regarding the creator of all worlds.
Some claim it is a mani-jewel, while others say it is gold, silver, or various other ores.
The differences in the colors of birds and beasts, the sharpness of thorns at their tips—these are all distinct;
one should know that there is no creator.
The various characteristics of the world arise entirely from conceptual discrimination.
Neither the Primal Nature (pradhāna) nor atoms, nor causelessness, nor spontaneity—
these are the false imaginings of those with evil discernment who do not know its essential nature.
They give rise to such conceptualizations as "it is karma" or "it is not karma."
Just as poison within milk, Transforms and corresponds with it,
So too are all phenomena distinguished In every respect;
this nature is neither born Nor does this nature ever perish.
Those who are deluded cannot comprehend the various diverse conceptualizations;
the world is merely an accumulation [of these], which only those established in meditative concentration can perceive.
You all should practice with diligence, realizing that there is no such thing as karma or non-karma apart from thought.
Sentient beings come and go to one another, like the sun and moon traversing their cycles;
dwelling in space without support, they revolve according to the wind.
The nature of karma is extremely subtle and hidden; only those of the Guhyasamāja can perceive it.
Practicing various superior contemplations, one is not greatly fettered;
like a great fire that burns for a long time, reducing everything to ashes in an instant,
so too should one know that the fire of wisdom consumes the fuel of karma in this very way.
Just as a lamp dispels darkness, exhausting it entirely in a single thought,
so too the darkness of habitual tendencies from all karma— the accumulation of perfumation since beginningless time—
is instantly and completely extinguished when the lamp of the Muni’s wisdom arises.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha again addressed the great assembly:
"It is like a desolate wilderness where one wishes to construct a palace."
A craftsman relies upon earth and wood, Only then can he bring [a house] to completion;
Yet when one observes closely among all things, Neither of these two possesses a dwelling.
It is also like a collection of fingers, Which, through their conjunction, form a fist.
If one seeks apart from the fingers, the substance of the fist cannot be found.
So too with the general and the chariot, the city and the grove,
the clouds, objects, mountains, and rivers, as well as the various characteristics of jars, garments, and so forth.
All are merely provisional combinations; the wise understand them to be like dreams.
Thus this body, a dwelling place, is an accumulation of the various elements (dhātus);
its aggregates (skandhas) are heaped up like a lofty mountain, yet it is as precarious and unstable as a dilapidated house.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither self nor other;
Like a city of Gandharvas, like clouds, and like shadows;
Furthermore, like a mirage in the heat, and like observing a painted scene.
Phenomenal marks manifest from delusion, yet their nature is pure and free from existence and non-existence.
It is like the blind and the lame, who must rely on one another to walk;
since their individual natures cannot sustain them alone, so too it is with the bodies of the ignorant.
When analyzed down to the ultimate atom, it is empty and lacks any real substance;
since the ultimate atom cannot be found, all phenomena are likewise so.
When a practitioner of yoga with pure wisdom reflects in this way,
One becomes detached from forms, sounds, and the like, and distances oneself from discursive thoughts;
when all mental activity has ceased, one attains liberation with profound composure.
Having no craving for sentient beings, one always delights in meditative equipoise.
Even if various celestial immortals and beautiful women should come to make offerings,
he regards them as if observing a dream, remaining untainted.
Though his body dwells here, those of external paths cannot perceive him.
Even the Vidyādharas and the Brahmās cannot behold his crown.
He shall be born in a palace of jewels, sporting with sovereign ease;
together with hosts of vidyā-consorts, he shall enjoy constant delight free from desire.
This method of contemplative practice is the domain of the sattvas;
you, O Benevolent One, should swiftly cultivate it. Arousing a courageous mind, you shall be born in the Palace of Radiance and bring benefit to those in the three realms of existence.
Then, having severed the portion of craving and abandoned hatred and delusion,
one is able to reach the Great Secret Adorned Land, that tranquil and sublime realm.
It is a state beyond death, and it is not within the sphere of ordinary consciousness.
Far removed from all signs, not to be attained through conceptual discrimination—
this is the subtle and wondrous state with which the yogin should be in accord.
Therefore, practicing the path of contemplation, one should aspire to that land.
Having overcome greed and anger, being without self and without person, you should cultivate supreme concentration; do not give rise to the three poisons.
If you cling to sensory objects, then dualistic perceptions will arise.
Just as when a beautiful woman, with a lovely face and glossy hair,
is seen by one full of desire; he becomes attached and dwells upon her,
giving rise to deluded and defiled thoughts, focusing his mind exclusively on her with no other thought.
Whether walking, coming, sitting, or rising, whether eating, drinking, or sleeping,
the form of that woman constantly appears within the mind’s perception.
Such evil wisdom arises entirely from delusive objects.
Sunk in the mire of sensory objects, one should therefore not be attached to them.
Just as those in the world, with their distorted wisdom and false discriminations,
[make distinctions] regarding cattle, goats, sheep, and deer.
Because one perceives that the ox has horns, one grasps it as being real;
yet regarding the tiger and the rabbit, one then gives rise to the understanding that they have no horns.
If one had not seen the horns on the ox, how could one grasp at the rabbit as being hornless?
The world is likewise thus: through false views one perceives things as obtainable;
yet later, when seeking their essence, they are found not to be real. Consequently, one declares that phenomena are definitively non-existent;
until one abandons conceptual discrimination, such false awakening will constantly arise.
The Benevolent One should carefully observe that the mental activities within all realms of experience are all like what is falsely apprehended, equal to horns and the absence of horns.
If practitioners can cultivate such an observation, [they shall realize the truth].
According to their respective inclinations, some become wheel-turning kings who travel back and forth through the air, endowed with great majestic power;
others are born in the palaces of the sun and moon, or in the mansions of the various lunar mansions.
The Four Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yāma and Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin; Within the palaces of mani jewels;
The bodies of the Brahmakāyika gods of the Form Realm, Along with the ten abodes of the Brahmā heavens.
The Heaven of No Affliction and the Heaven of No Heat, Sudarśana and Sudarśanīya, And the palace of Akaniṣṭha, where they sport with mastery;
The realms of Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, and Nothingness, And that of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
Abiding therein, one gradually eliminates desire, And even throughout all Buddha-fields,
Constantly dwells in subtle meditative concentration, The realm of liberation.
Just as when a jar is broken, It becomes shards of pottery;
The nature of disintegration manifests in each moment; while perceiving permanence, one encounters impermanence.
From the seed the sprout arises, yet by the time the sprout is born, the seed has already perished.
It is just as when a potter fashions a jar from clay.
If the clay is of a certain color, the jar will likewise be of that color;
sometimes the potter uses clay of various colors,
and by the time it has been fired, each follows the color of its respective clay.
From *jiantu* bamboo grow onions; from *jiao* bamboo grow garlic.
From filth flies and from spoiled honey, various insects are born.
One should know that the fruits of the world may resemble their causes, or they may not.
Because all things undergo transformation and decay, they are able to produce effects;
yet the various atoms that constitute these works do not themselves undergo transformation or decay.
It is only the ignorant of the world who give rise to false conceptualizations.
That which can act as my inner self, a superior self, is unattainable;
nor is there a self in the mind, nor a cause of accumulation,
nor a cause of direct production, for it does not exist conditioned by consciousness.
The realm of the wise is born from the power of skillful means;
it uproots the thorns of affliction and subdues Māra along with his retinue.
Worldly craving is exhausted, just as honey causes [the body] to waste away.
Because the various sages possess craving, they transmigrate through the various realms of existence;
long habituated by it, they are like snakes full of venom.
Scorched by the fire of afflictions, they wander through the perilous and evil destinies.
Freedom from craving is liberation; one should always diligently cultivate contemplative practice.

In the past, through the power of the Buddha, I was sustained by his empowerment and attained wondrous samādhi.
I clearly beheld millions of lands and those who practice worldly concentrations.
The Buddhas and their sons, the pure abodes where they dwell—
Among these, only the Guhyasamāja is supreme bliss;
the Buddhas sit upon lotuses as if within most exquisite palaces.
We have arisen from meditative absorption and gaze with single-minded devotion.
I see myself dwelling in Ghanavyūha, surrounded by a multitude of Buddha-sons.
Again, I see the Treasury of Liberation dwelling within a palace;
its body is the size of a finger-joint, and its physical form is most brilliantly radiant.
Like the pure full moon in the sky, like the aghana-saṃjñaka flower,
I thought to myself:
"Whose is this inconceivable deed?"
Even though one's own body is seen within that womb,

the sons of the Lotus-Treasury Buddha [perceive this].
They all saw it in this way, and everyone marveled at the inconceivable.

The various colors of the *yoginī* are the realm of the Buddha. You,
O virtuous ones, should know that in the past, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva,

The Radiant and the Blazing Wisdom, the Difficult to Conquer and the Manifest,

Give rise to faith and do not harbor doubt;

Sometimes he becomes a lord of the gods, or one of the minor kings;

Just as a skilled physician can cure all diseases,
so too is the Awakened One able to eliminate the sickness of delusion.
Having attained a mind free from discrimination, he remains unmoved even if his limbs were to be severed.
Regarding all internal and external objects, one thoroughly realizes they are but consciousness;
thus one is able to distance oneself from the self and likewise from what belongs to the self.
There is neither the harmer nor the harmed, nor the instruments of harm.
All these are entirely within the sphere of the mental consciousness;
all depend upon the ālayavijñāna, thus giving rise to false discrimination.
Just as when a gem meets the sunlight, fire is produced through their mutual resonance.
This fire does not emerge from the jewel, nor does it arise from the sun.

Mind, intellect, and consciousness are likewise: through the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and the mental organ, they give rise to all states of mind, just as waves arise upon the ocean.
This nature is not a mirage, nor is it like a dream or an illusion;
it is not the same as those things grasped through delusion,
nor is it like the hair of a tortoise or a frog, or the horns of a rabbit.
Furthermore, when thunder and lightning combine, they strike and produce fire.
As for this fire, one can never definitively know whether it originates from the water or from the thunder and lightning; there is no certainty regarding its place of origin.
Just as fire arises from water to produce jars and the like,
so too do the mental factors such as desire arise simultaneously with the mind;
being a composite without a fixed nature, they should be known to be just like this.
The inconceivable state of mind is known and seen by those of the Ghanavyūha;
it is the treasury that protects sentient beings, primordially and wondrously co-emergent,
like nirvāṇa and space, and of the nature of unconditioned analytical cessation.
Transcending the three periods of time, it is pure and eternally perfect.
Like the moon with its waning and waxing, it manifests throughout all lands;
though its cycles appear as one, its nature neither increases nor decreases.
Ordinary people discriminate and perceive the moon as waxing and waning,
coming and going across the four continents, yet in reality it has neither fullness nor deficiency.
So too is this storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which universally manifests throughout the realm of sentient beings.
Its essence neither increases nor decreases, being perfectly pure and ever-luminous;
yet the deluded, through false discrimination, constantly conceive of increase and decrease within the ālayavijñāna— know that it is likewise so.
If one can correctly and thoroughly understand this consciousness,
one will immediately attain the state of outflow-free purity and the distinctions of the stage of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Such distinguished dharmas as these are extremely difficult to obtain.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise; it evolves together with the seven consciousnesses.
While it is associated with habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), its essential nature remains undefiled.
It is like a piece of wood in a river, drifting along as it follows the current.
Yet as wood flows with the current, its substance and form remain distinct;
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which, though accompanied by the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of all the cognitions,
is eternally pure in nature and is not defiled by their activities.
Purity and defilement both depend upon the ālayavijñāna;
The noble ones’ experience of bliss in the present life, The state of meditative equipoise,
The various realms of humans and gods, And all the buddha-fields— [all arise from it].
Thus, these phenomena of defilement and purity have the Tathāgatagarbha as their cause;
through awakening to it, one becomes a Buddha, serving as the seed-nature for all vehicles.
All sentient beings possess this sovereign power.
All sovereign virtues and all supreme auspiciousness,
even in perilous and evil places, throughout the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior— within these,
the ālayavijñāna constantly dwells, universally serving as their support.
All these sentient beings are the fruits of beginningless time;
through the habitual tendencies of various karmas, they are able to increase themselves,
and likewise cause the remaining seven consciousnesses to increase as well.
Because of this, foolish people grasp at it as an internal self, an agent, and a basis; thus they wander through birth and death.
Consciousness within the body whirls as swiftly as the turning of the wind.
Blown and stirred by the winds of karma, it dwells pervasively within all the sense faculties;
always accompanied by the seven consciousnesses, it flows and turns like waves.
[The theories of] atoms, the Primal Nature (prakṛti), the Lord (īśvara), time, and space— [All these are likewise refuted.]
All these are the pure ālayavijñāna, within which false discrimination arises.
Through the power of karma and with craving as its cause,
the ālaya brings about the accomplishment of all worlds and their various categories.
Fools never comprehend it, yet they cling to it as a creator.
The essence and characteristics of this consciousness are subtle and extremely difficult to know;
not having seen the reality, their minds are deluded and unable to awaken.
"Constantly toward the faculties, objects, and the mind, they give rise to craving and attachment.
Vajragarbha spoke again:
"O fearless sons of the Buddha!"
Thus, as for the essence of the ālayavijñāna, why is it neither seen nor heard?
It is the support of all bodies, pure by nature and eternally unstained;
it is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Buddha as well as those of a wheel-turning monarch.
Pervading throughout the triple world, it manifests in various forms.
Just as the pure moon in the sky is surrounded by a multitude of stars,
so too do the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the various consciousnesses abide within the body.
Just as the Lord of the Desire Realm, surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens,
manifests within his precious palace, so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Like the various deities of rivers and seas who move with sovereign ease amidst the waters, [so does the ālayavijñāna abide].
The ālayavijñāna abides in the world; know that it is likewise so.
As a dragon depends on water, as the heavens depend on the sky, as the hundred rivers flow toward the sea, and as the king of trees depends upon the earth—so too does the manifesting mind abide.
Like the sun within its palace, circling Mount Sumeru, All the devas pay it homage; such is the mind on the stage of Buddhahood.
Within the ten stages, one practices all the deeds.
Abiding within the body of a bodhisattva, they manifest throughout the great ocean;
universally benefiting and bringing peace and happiness, they are constantly praised by the Tathāgata.
As each stage becomes purified, they are thus called "Sons of the Buddha."
Residing within the body of a bodhisattva, this is precisely what is called a "bodhisattva.
Both the Buddhas and all bodhisattvas are designated by the name Ālaya.
The Buddhas and the supreme sons [of the Buddha] have already received or shall receive their predictions [of enlightenment].
The vast ālaya shall become perfectly awakened;
this very essence of the ālaya is seen by those of the Guhyasamāja,
because they are conjoined with sublime meditative concentration through the most excellent yoga.
The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and even those non-Buddhists who have realized the truth and attained fearlessness— all that they perceive is this consciousness.
The various objects of all these consciousnesses are all transformations of the mind.
Objects such as jars and garments—such natures do not exist at all;
they all depend upon the ālayavijñāna. All that is perceived is delusion;
through various habitual tendencies (vāsanās), one falsely gives rise to the grasped and the grasper.
The essence is not like a magical illusion, nor like a mirage or a hair-circle;
it is neither born nor unborn. It is emptiness, empty and utterly remote;
both existence and non-existence lack intrinsic nature, and the same applies to long and short, and so forth.
When the wise observe illusory phenomena, they see that these are all merely magical illusions;
not a single thing has ever arisen that is identical to the illusion itself.
That which sentient beings conceptualize is visible like an illusion.
The appearance of a mirage and the appearance of hair-tufts—both are unattainable;
apart from one, there is no second. There is nothing past and nothing present.
All these are transformations of consciousness; there is neither illusion nor the name "illusion."
All natures are unapprehendable; they are illusions and the products of illusion.
There is delusion in the world, and their minds lack self-mastery;
they falsely claim there is a "magician" who creates various things through illusion.
Though movement and coming-and-going are seen, they are all not real;
Just as iron shifts its direction because of a magnet,
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise, Following the seeds of conceptual discrimination.
Throughout all worlds, there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Like the sun or a mani jewel, it is without thought or discrimination;
this consciousness pervades all places, and its manifestation is called transmigration.
Neither dying nor being born, fundamentally not a phenomenon of saṃsāra,
like seeing birth and death in a dream— upon awakening, there is liberation.
If a son of the Buddha undergoes this transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), he is then called one who is liberated.
This is precisely the most supreme teaching and principle of all Buddhas:
to examine all phenomena as one would with a scale, as one would with a clear mirror,
to illuminate them like a bright lamp, and to test them like gold and stone.
The characteristic mark of the true path is to remain far removed from annihilationism.
Those who cultivate supreme meditative concentration do so through pure causes;
by being freed from all defilements, they manifest the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The Mahāyāna-Guhyakapada-Sūtra, Volume Lower.
[By] Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si Te-jin Shi Hong-lu Qing.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—Grand Master of Great Wisdom, conferred the title of Grand Preceptor (Sikong), bestowed purple robes, granted the posthumous name "Great Mirror" (Dajian), and enfeoffed as Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households—by Imperial Decree. Chapter Seven: The Sphere of My Own Consciousness (Part Two). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions. From the jewel within his topknot, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated all worlds, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin deities, and the assembly of Buddha-sons within the Ghanavyūha realm.
Having emitted this light, he immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvabuddhadharmatathatādarśana, saying:
"O Lord of Beings!

Within the Snowy Mountains there is a malevolent beast named 'The Harmful. It employs hundreds of thousands of deceptive stratagems to capture various animals; it kills and devours those that are fit for food."
If it sees a powerful beast named "Neng" (Capable), it must immediately imitate the sound of calling its own offspring to harm and devour it;
if it occasionally sees a horned beast, it manifests horns to resemble it and approaches with intimacy so as not to let the feared one kill and eat it;
seeing various beasts such as oxen and sheep, it assumes their very forms to carry out its depredations.
O Benevolent Lord!

Just as those harmful beings manifest various forms to kill wild beasts, so too it is with all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): they give rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) based on the *ālayavijñāna* and cling to the characteristics of a self (*ātma-nimitta*). Like malevolent beasts that transform into various forms, they likewise conceive of a self within their respective categories, each distinct from the others, even down to the smallest, like a mote of dust.
“O Lord of Benevolence!
Upon what do these various forms of self-grasping depend for their existence?
They do not abide elsewhere, but abide solely within consciousness.”
Those who maintain the view of a self say:
"The arising of consciousness occurs through the conjunction of the self, the mental faculty, and the object; fundamentally, there is no self.
It is like when a flower and a garment are joined, there is fragrance; if they are not joined, the garment has no scent.
Therefore, one should know that there is only consciousness, consisting of the mind and its mental factors; apart from consciousness, there is no self among the mind and its mental factors.

Just as fruit within a vessel, a lamp illuminating a jar, or the *iṣīkā* grass and the *mañca* grass may be perceived, so too do the mind and its mental factors arise solely through causes and conditions.
Within this, there is neither self nor arising; it is a subtle, singular mark, primordially quiescent.
This is the sphere of self-realization for the practitioner of superior insight who has attained awakening.

Just as those malevolent beasts cause much injury and slaughter, so too are the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas): they nurture and increase the evil views of the world; lacking knowledge of the Dharma and wisdom, they forcibly engage in conceptual discrimination, grasping at existence and non-existence, at unity and multiplicity, and at the theories of "self" and "what belongs to self."
Why is this so? It is because they do not awaken to the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

Driven by craving and false wisdom, they wander to and fro, rushing through the cycle of birth and death; they distance themselves from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends; they oppose liberation and cause their right wisdom to waver; they are unable to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, and thus they have no realization whatsoever regarding the three vehicles, even up to the one vehicle.
"Because they give rise to attachment and fail to see the Noble Truths, they do not even hear the name of Ghanavyūha, let alone enter that land.
O Lord of Beings!"
All those who dwell in profound meditative concentrations have completely purified their view of self within this consciousness.

You and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should likewise do so; having diligently cultivated it yourselves, you should also explain it to others, enabling them to swiftly enter the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha.
At that time, Vajragarbha, in order to clarify this storehouse consciousness—
the very meaning of the Secret Adornment— addressed Yathārthadarśin, saying:
"Just as a magnet attracts iron and is itself constantly moved by it;
Just as the nature of a chariot made of aggregates is fixed, yet its movement arises from habitual tendencies;
and just as grass, wood, earth, bamboo, and so forth, together with ropes,
form a house that is visible through their combination— so too are the body and the aggregates.
"A reanimated corpse, a magnet, and iron move as if they possessed sentience;
all things are likewise thus—the aggregates are without self.
Then the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi addressed King Viśva-varṇa:
“O King, you should now question the Vajragarbha who is in meditative absorption:
‘Regarding all that exists in all worlds, what is it that you do not perceive, yet is apart from perception; that which is utterly beyond all verbal expression?’”
Regarding the names of the two types— correspondence and non-correspondence—
and how the self-nature of all that exists in the world abides:
may all the sons of the Buddhas in this assembly listen with single-minded devotion.
The King of Supreme Form then asked in accordance with the meaning:
"Regarding the objects of names, marks, and so forth— all worldly phenomena—
are they merely conceptual constructions?"
"Does it exist apart from conceptual construction?
If it exists according to the names established for it, upon what do those names depend?
Having heard this, Vajragarbha immediately addressed the King of Form:
"All things exist as mere names, established solely through conceptual designation;
because they differ from the designating expressions, the designated objects cannot be found.
The four aggregates are merely names, and for this reason they are called 'names'."
Just as the name "Māṇava" exists as a mere name without any substantial entity,
so too do the Buddhas and their heirs teach that names exist only in dependence upon characteristics (*nimitta*).
Apart from characteristics, a name cannot be discerned or differentiated.
Therefore, based upon various characteristics, one discriminates various names;
like the hare’s horn or a barren woman’s son, these provisional names cannot be found.
Within characteristics there is nothing at all, yet the deluded falsely discriminate.
The world is also like this: devoid of characteristics, it has no name.
Vases, garments, vehicles, and the like are merely conceptualized through names and words;
though names and characteristics can be spoken of, their essential nature does not exist.
All the various phenomena of the world consist only of marks and nothing more;
names are established solely based upon these marks, and thus they are said to lack substantial reality.
Your Majesty should observe that worldly phenomena exist apart from names, for nothing exists independently of them.
It is only through the discriminating mind that grasping and attachment arise.
If one is free from discrimination, grasping and attachment will not arise;
where there is no arising, there is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), and one realizes the inexhaustible Dharma.
Therefore, Great Kings, you should always contemplate that all things are merely the discriminating mind;
apart from this, nothing exists. The growth of forms and bodies, as well as their dissolution and the sustenance of the physical frame, [are likewise but the mind].
Such various names as these are all merely conceptualizations of form.
The name, the conceptualization, and the discrimination—their essential nature is fundamentally no different;
yet, in accordance with worldly conventions, they are established under different names.
If one sets aside names and seeks for the substance of things, it cannot be found in either the past or the future.
It is merely the transformation of the various consciousnesses; there is no dharma that is known.
That which is known is merely a name; such is the nature of the entire world.
One discriminates phenomena by means of names, yet phenomena do not correspond to those names.
The nature of all phenomena is thus: they do not abide within discrimination.
Since phenomena are merely names, their characteristics have no intrinsic substance;
when characteristics are absent, names are also absent—where, then, could conceptualization exist?
If one attains non-conceptuality, body and mind are eternally tranquil.
Just as wood, once consumed by fire, never grows back again; so too,
like a person carrying a burden, one is called a "burden-bearer," and according to the differences in the burden, there are distinctions among those who bear it.
The name is like the object carried; the conceptualization is the carrier.
Because names are manifold, the conceptualizations are each different.
It is like seeing a stump as a person, or seeing a person as a stump.
The person and the post are two conceptual constructions; they exist merely as names.
Within the combination of the great elements, one conceptually constructs "form," yet apart from these great elements, its substance can never be found.
Just as a quality depends on a jar for its location, so too does a jar depend on its name;
yet when one seeks the jar apart from these, the jar can never be found.
Since a jar does not abide within the substance of a jar, how could a name possibly abide within a name?
The two arise from conceptual construction; even names and measures do not exist.
Abiding in such a meditative concentration, one’s mind does not waver.
Just as gold, stone, and the like have no inherent characteristic of water from the very beginning, so it is with this state.
Just as fire is conjoined with its fuel, Or as water flows and moves,
So too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna): Its essence is not itself a phenomenon of transmigration,
Yet when in mutual association with the various consciousnesses, It flows along together with those phenomena.
Just as iron, due to a magnet, revolves and moves about,
though neither possesses volition, yet appears as if it did;
so too should one know that the ālayavijñāna and the seven consciousnesses are likewise.
Dragged by the ropes of habitual tendencies, though insubstantial it appears as if real;
pervading the bodies of sentient beings, it wanders through perilous realms,
like iron drawn to a magnet, revolving without mutual awareness.
Some leave the perilous realms and attain the stages;
through the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations, such as the Śūraṅgama Samādhi which is like an illusion,
and even up to the dhāraṇīs, there is nothing they do not fully accomplish.
Praising the Buddha’s true merits constitutes an offering.
He may manifest infinite bodies, with a single body possessing infinite hands;
from shoulders, heads, mouths, and tongues, each extending further until they are all infinite.
They travel to the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Tathāgatas,
raining down flowers and robes, as well as crowns and necklaces;
with various precious ornaments piled up like Mount Sumeru.
Making offerings to omniscience, to the Buddhas and their sons;
or creating jeweled palaces like clouds arrayed in myriad colors,
manifesting celestial maidens who dwell and move within them.
With the exquisite sounds of music and song, they make offerings to all Buddhas.
Sometimes they travel and dwell always in the company of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
all demonic adversaries they subdue with sovereign ease.
Having attained the noble wisdom of self-awakening, adorned with right concentration,
and having already transformed the basis, one perceives the selflessness of phenomena—
the five dharmas, the three natures, and the eight consciousnesses.
Able to accomplish all vidyās, dwelling in meditative concentration, they constantly make offerings.
Sometimes manifesting bodies vast and expansive, and sometimes appearing as small as motes of dust,
with various kinds of physical forms, they make offerings to all Buddhas.
Sometimes the body contains all lands, and lands enter into a mustard seed;
the great ocean becomes a cow’s footprint, or a cow’s footprint becomes the sea;
yet the sentient beings therein experience no oppression or distress.
Impartially bestowing material provisions, like the earth and the sun and moon,
like water, fire, and wind, like a jewel island and wondrous medicine,
they are universally able to bring benefit and nurture all sentient beings.
All phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, Neither interrupted nor eternal,
Neither identical nor different, Neither coming nor going;
To falsely establish various names for them Is what constitutes the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
All phenomena are like illusions, Like dreams, cities of the gandharvas,
Mirages, the moon in water, A whirling firebrand, clouds, and thunder.
That which is falsely grasped therein Is the nature of universal imagination (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Through various names that express, one designates various phenomena;
yet these are not to be found therein—this is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
All worldly phenomena do not transcend name and form (*nāma-rūpa*).
If one is separated from the designator, the designated cannot be found;
such is the nature of pervasive conceptualization, which I call the world.
With the eye, forms, and so forth as conditions, it arises through the conjunction of these three.
Sound issues forth from drums and their mallets; Sprouts grow from seeds in the earth.
Palaces, jars, and garments— These arise from various conditions without a [permanent] substratum.
Sentient beings and all phenomena— All these are of the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
If a dharma is untainted (anāsrava), its meaning cannot be abandoned;
it is the realm of the noble self-realized wisdom, and this nature is called "endowed with reality.
Having already explained the distinctions between the characteristics of all dharmas and their intrinsic natures, [I shall now explain]...
If separated from the gate of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all phenomena are not clearly manifest.
Just as when various objects are combined, they manifest as illusory forms;
though their many colors differ, their nature is in every case indeterminate.
All worldly affairs are exactly like this; Of various kinds, none are real.
They are what deluded sentiments grasp at, A pervasive conceptualization with nothing remaining [of reality].
It is like a mani jewel, In which images appear according to the colors [that reflect it].
The world is likewise so: it exists only through conceptual construction;
its essence and function have no location—this is the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Like a city of Gandharvas, it is not a city yet appears as one.
Nor is it without a cause that one can thus perceive the various things of the world;
know that it is likewise so for the palaces of the sun and moon, the various mountains, and the jeweled peaks.
Smoke and clouds strike against one another, yet they have never been in disarray;
they share no commonality and possess no intrinsic nature. Their essential nature is entirely non-existent;
they are merely what is conceptually constructed—the nature of pervasive imagination.
All things are not born from causes, nor do they arise without a cause;
whether existent or non-existent, these are all attachments of the mind.
Names arise in dependence upon signs, and both [names and signs] are produced from conceptual construction.
Right knowledge and suchness are far removed from conceptual construction;
the mind appears as its own marks, and these marks serve as the support for the manas.
The manas and the five consciousnesses arise together, like waves upon the ocean.
Vāsanās have no beginning, and so too are their objects;
the mind arises from vāsanās, while objects cause the mind to be deluded and confused.
Depending upon the ālayavijñāna, all seeds [reside].
When the mind appears as objective realms, this is called the world;
the seven consciousnesses and the ālayavijñāna arise from one another in mutual succession.
Thus, these eight kinds of consciousness are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation.
All the worlds appear to be arranged as if they truly exist.
Some reckon that all sentient beings— through the conjunction of the self, the sense organs,
and their objects— give rise to various consciousnesses that discern and differentiate all objective realms.
Some falsely reckon that because the agent is the cause of karma, one is born in the Brahma-heaven and other realms, as well as in all internal and external worlds.
Yet these worlds are not made by an agent; they are produced by karma and atoms.
However, the ālayavijñāna manifests as if it were an object;
the store-consciousness is not produced by conditions, nor is the store-consciousness not produced by conditions.
Although the various consciousnesses flow and circulate, there is no triadic conjunction.
The essence of the ālayavijñāna is eternally abiding, with the various consciousnesses accompanying it;
like a wheel and a crystal, or like the stars together with the moon,
from this arise habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which grow ever anew.
Furthermore, as subsequent lifetimes increase, so too do subsequent consciousnesses;
thus do birth and death revolve, yet for the awakened one, the mind does not revolve.
It is like fire burning wood, shifting and changing gradually.
Once this wood has been burned, it further burns other wood;
so too is the untainted mind in relation to the *ālayavijñāna*.
Gradually eliminating all that is tainted, it brings the phenomena of saṃsāra to eternal rest.
This is the bliss of the present life, the accomplishment of samādhi;
from this the noble ones are born, traveling from realm to realm.
It is like exquisite gold that cannot be seen while it remains within its ore.
Just as a wise smith skillfully smelts and refines it, so that the gold becomes manifest;

the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise: though entangled by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), when purified through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the awakened one perceives it ever clearly.
Just as cream cannot be obtained from curd unless it is churned and stirred, so too the wise churn the curd to obtain the butter.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise: it is enveloped and concealed by the various evolving consciousnesses.
Those who practice the various meditative concentrations of Ghanavyūha attain them through diligent contemplation.
Ghanavyūha is the Great Illumination, a sublime designation for wondrous wisdom;
the sons of the Buddha who diligently cultivate it will be born within this realm.
In the realms of form and formlessness— The spheres of space, consciousness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
Having constantly and diligently practiced therein, They have come to be born in this place.
Among these sons of the Buddhas here, Their majestic radiance is like that of the sun and moon.
Through practice one attains right concentration and expounds the corresponding path;
all Buddhas bestow empowerment and together confer upon one that station.
Regarding the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, one transforms the basis in accordance with what is seen.
"Though dwelling within the field of Ghanavyūha, he manifests transformations in response to beings;
according to their inclinations and preferences for the Dharma, he abides in emptiness and expounds it.
At that time, Vajragarbha again addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The ālayavijñāna, from time immemorial, has been perfumed by conceptual proliferation;
bound by various karmas, it revolves without end.
It is just like the great ocean, which gives rise to waves because of the wind."
Constantly arising and constantly ceasing, Neither interrupted nor permanent,
Because one does not realize one’s own mind, The realms of consciousness appear accordingly.
If one understands one’s own mind, It is like fire consuming wood until it is exhausted.
One who penetrates the outflow-free is called a sage.
The storehouse consciousness transforms into manifold objects, pervading and encompassing the world;
the manas clings to "self" and "what belongs to self," its deliberations constantly flowing on.
The various categories of consciousness each cognize their own respective objects;
that which accumulates karma is called *citta*, that which universally accumulates is called *manas*, and that which discriminates is called *vijñāna*; the five consciousnesses grasp present objects.
Like one with cataracts seeing a net of hairs, one is deluded by what is seen;
within a mind that resembles form, one perceives form where there is no form.
It is like a mani jewel, illuminated by the light of the sun and moon.
Appearing according to what is appropriate, each rains down things of its own kind.
So too is the ālayavijñāna, the Tathāgata’s pure storehouse;
conjoined with habitual tendencies, it manifests throughout the world.
Associated with the untainted, it rains down all dharmas of merit.
Just as milk undergoes transformation, becoming curd and then whey,
so too does the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) transform, appearing as various forms.
Just as one with cataracts sees falling hairs, so too do sentient beings;
obscured by the cataracts of negative habitual tendencies dwelling within the eye of the *ālayavijñāna*,
they perceive these various forms in places where no form exists.
It is like a mirage, far removed from existence and non-existence.
What appears through the habituation of the ālayavijñāna—O Noble One, based upon the eye and forms, a consciousness resembling form arises; it dwells within the eye like a magical illusion.
Fluttering like a shimmering mirage, all forms are but the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Corresponding with the habitual tendencies of form, they manifest as if having a substantial body, though that body does not exist.
Fools engage in false discrimination, mired in various states of delusion and negligence.
Sitting, reclining, and running about wildly, as well as the sudden arising of all various activities—
all these depend upon the *ālayavijñāna*.
When light spreads and shines upon the ground, its steaming vapor appears like flowing water.
Just as thirsty beasts run toward a mirage, so too is the ālayavijñāna: its essential nature is truly not form, yet it appears as if it were form.
The arising of false and evil perceptions is like a magnet attracting iron.
Swiftly shifting and transferring, though devoid of mental consciousness,
it moves as if possessing consciousness.
Ensnared by birth and death, it wanders through the various realms of existence.
Not-self yet resembling the self,
without thought it flows along with the stream; the *ālaya* is non-conceptual,
moving in dependence upon the body.
"Just as when two elephants fight, the one wounded retreats forever;
so too is the ālayavijñāna: when defilements are severed, there is no further transmigration.
Just as a pure lotus flower is bright and clean, being free from the mud,"
Both humans and devas enjoy [it], and there are none who do not treasure and revere it.

So too is this ālayavijñāna: having emerged from the mire of habitual tendencies (vāsanā), through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) it attains purity, and is thus held in high esteem by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Just as a supreme jewel may be held in contempt by a rustic,
yet when used to adorn a ceremonial crown, it is worn upon the head of a king;
so too is the ālaya-vijñāna, which is the pure Buddha-nature.
The stage of ordinary beings is ever defiled, while the fruit of Buddhahood is eternally maintained as a treasure.
Like a fine jade submerged in water, shrouded and covered by mossy growth, the ālayavijñāna dwells within birth and death; entangled by habitual tendencies, it does not manifest.
Within this ālayavijñāna, two modes of grasping arise,
like a snake with two heads that moves together according to its will.
The ālaya is likewise, endowed with all manner of phenomenal forms.
All the worlds take [form] as their color. Those with false perceptions are deluded,
reckoning it as "I" and "mine," whether existent or non-existent, claiming that a sovereign creator made the world.
Although the ālayavijñāna manifests transformations, its essential nature is eternally profound;
to those ignorant people, it cannot be fully realized or understood.
It is like a master illusionist who conjures various kinds of beasts through magic.
Whether walking or running, they appear to have sentience yet lack reality.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise; it conjures up the world through illusion, and all sentient beings therein are devoid of any true essence.
Ordinary fools cannot comprehend this; they give rise to false grasping and attachment,
conceiving of atoms, a primal nature (prakṛti), existence and non-existence, various dualistic discriminations,
as well as the views of Brahmā, the Great Man (puruṣa), and so forth.
All conceptualizations are of the mind; one conceptualizes within the world.
These views of conceptualization are fundamentally without reality.
They are like figures in a painting, or like the appearance of a rainbow.
And objects within the clouds, The floating hairs seen by those with cataracts,
A woman gazing at her reflection in a mirror, Like dreaming while observing various forms,
Like a rainbow in the sky or an echo in a valley, Tree shadows and the city of the Gandharvas.
As a mirage appears as water in the heat, or as the moon’s reflection in a pond—
such conceptual constructions are falsely grasped within the ālayavijñāna.
When these are examined, one realizes with certainty that they are nothing but the storehouse consciousness.
One immediately realizes the characteristics of the world, and all dharmas upon which it relies—
all these views of conceptual discrimination— thereby cease and vanish. The ālaya-vijñāna,
along with the manas and the other [vijñānas], is the basis for the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of all dharmas.
Constantly engaged in discrimination, the mind is agitated and turbid.
If one is free from discrimination, one immediately realizes the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga),
which is eternal and unchanging, just like space.
If one attains samādhi regarding the ālayavijñāna,
then the untainted dharmas will arise: the concentrations at will,
the liberations, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, and skillfulness.
With mastery and supernormal powers, and all such virtues as these,
one gives rise to the ten ultimate vows; the mind-made,
subtle body eternally transforms its basis, and the realm of consciousness dwells forever in peace.
Its essence is identical to the nature of empty space; it is neither destroyed nor exhausted.
The Tathāgata perceives this clearly: in the world there is neither increase nor decrease, sentient beings do not arise anew, and nirvāṇa is not annihilation.
This world-system and all other world-systems are identical in their single dharmatā.
Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the dharmatā is primordially and eternally abiding;
it is neither permanent nor subject to annihilation.
Furthermore, if those who are liberated were to cause the cessation of the realm of sentient beings,
they would destroy the Tathāgata’s nature of all-encompassing wisdom and the sphere of the Buddhas of the three times, and thus fail to attain equality.
Furthermore, if parinirvāṇa were the extinction of the realm of sentient beings,
who would be liberated from suffering, attain the state with remainder or without remainder,
and subdue Māra and wrong views?
All such [assertions] must be false teachings.
Therefore, one should know that for those superior practitioners of insight who have realized liberation, their bodies abide eternally.
Forever free from the aggregates of grasping, All habitual tendencies are extinguished.
Just as when a red-hot iron Is cast into cold water,
Although the heat has been removed, The substance of the iron remains unimpaired.
O virtuous ones, you should know that the ālayavijñāna is like the ocean;
constantly struck by the winds of coarse afflictions and conceptual proliferation,
the waves of the five dharmas and the three natures arise in continuous succession.
All that exists within the sphere of objects, Its characteristics flickering and shifting, Within this realm of meaninglessness, Appears as meaning though lacking reality.
If one awakens to this, all is empty; The transformation of the basis is eternally inexhaustible.
Abiding in Ghanavyūha like the moon, its reflection appears throughout the ten directions.
One should know that the ālayavijñāna moves through the dense forest of the aggregates,
with manas as its vanguard and the mental consciousness capable of definitive discernment.
All objects such as form, as well as the five groups of consciousness,
in conjunction with the sense faculties and their objects, cognize present phenomena.
That which is grasped as its own object is entirely the ālayavijñāna.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), along with vitality, warmth, and the nature of contact, are in a state of integration.
The manas depends upon this consciousness, and that consciousness in turn dwells within the mind (manas).
The remaining five types of consciousness likewise dwell within their own respective sense organs.
The mind, the mental faculty, and the various consciousnesses dwell within the aggregates;
bound by the fetters of karmic habituation, they transmigrate without end. All such karma arises from craving.
Having already received a body through karma, one further creates karma with that body.
Having abandoned this body, one receives yet another;
thus, depending on causes from past to present, one crawls slowly like a leech.
The mind and its various mental factors arise in succession within the various realms of existence;
further accumulating one after another, they dwell within the dense forest of the aggregates.
When life-force, warmth, and consciousness depart from the body, [the body becomes cold and rigid].
The body is devoid of sensation, Just like wood or stone.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the mind (citta); That which clings to a self is called the intellect (manas).
That which can apprehend various objects Is therefore called consciousness (vijñāna).
The mind (*citta*) performs the act of collecting; the intellect (*manas*) acts as the universal collector;
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to discern universally, while the five sensory consciousnesses manifest discrimination.
The mind is able to sustain the body, while the *manas* clings to the various realms of existence.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to cognize universally; the five [sensory] consciousnesses take their own respective objects as conditions.
With the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their cause, the other consciousnesses arise from it.
The objects of the mind and mental consciousness flow on in uninterrupted succession.
The five consciousnesses further depend upon an additional dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to arise;
this is because their simultaneous own-sense bases (*svendriya*) act as that dominant condition.
This body is like a reanimated corpse and is also like a mirage in the heat.
Evolving in accordance with causes and conditions, it is neither false nor real;
led by sensation, its nature is empty and devoid of self.
The various evolving consciousnesses, such as the mental faculty, arise simultaneously with the mind.
The five consciousnesses further rely upon it, and the mental consciousness arises based on it;
thus, at all times, they revolve together with the universal ground (mahābhūmi).
The ālayavijñāna, being perfumed by craving, increases and grows.
Once they have grown themselves, they further increase the other consciousnesses;
revolving without interruption, they are like a waterwheel.
Because these consciousnesses exist, the various realms of existence arise.
Thus, within the various realms of existence, consciousness further undergoes growth;
consciousness and worldly phenomena act as mutual causes for one another.
It is like the flow of a river, which continues uninterrupted from beginning to end.
Just as a sprout and its seed arise in succession,
each distinct in its own particularity yet clearly manifest,
so too it is with the consciousness of formations: once the three have come together, they arise.
Furthermore, they again come together, arising with differentiated characteristics; thus they circulate, never ceasing.
All internal and external phenomena arise because of this.
"Fools do not understand that [all is] mind-only; you all should diligently observe this.
Then the King of Multicolored Forms and the others spoke thus again to Vajragarbha:
Skillfully entering the Secret Adorned Realm (*Guhyasamāja*), he can expound all dharmas;
the Buddha and his sons of enlightenment contemplate with right concentration—
this is incomparable and most extraordinary, clearly illuminating the characteristics of phenomena.
Vajragarbha, free from fear, deign to look upon us and proclaim [the teaching].
You dwell in a palace of mani-jewels, seated upon a supreme lion throne,
surrounded by the most excellent sons of the Victor, as you enter the Samādhi of Ghanavyūha.
I pray that for the sake of all these sons of the Buddha, you will expound the supreme Dharma of Yoga.
This is the teaching opened and proclaimed by the Buddha Candradhvaja for the assembly;
that assembly shall come here, so I pray you speak without weariness.
This Tathāgata Candradhvaja likewise manifests many miraculous transformations;
within the palaces of the desire realm and throughout the form realm,
he is surrounded by the sons of the Buddha, with all the devas attending upon him.
Having heard this exposition of the supreme method— the fearless Dharma of the *Ghanavyūha*—
those practitioners of yoga attain the noble wisdom of self-realization, the realm of internal personal experience.
Fearing the realm of *niraya* and the bliss of the fixed stage (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
they do not abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). While observing one another within meditative concentration,
they each think to themselves:
"Who has already realized the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*)? Who is the foremost among those who practice contemplation?
We pray that we may behold such a person.
With single-minded devotion, this assembly further reflected once more:
"What is concentration? What is non-concentration?
And upon what is one concentrated?"
Furthermore, by what dharma do they rely as the object-condition for meditative concentration?
Upon what do those sons of the Buddhas concentrate?
Behold within the land of Ghanavyūha the pure and most excellent sons of the Buddha.
The king of the assembly of Bodhisattvas, with a precious crown upon his head,
is adorned with the thirty-two marks and the secondary characteristics.
All have arisen from their meditative absorption, wearing exquisite jewel necklaces;
from immeasurable Buddha-lands, they have come to this assembly,
and with a single mind, they gaze up at Vajragarbha.
The powerful lords of yoga all contemplated this;
having attained the bliss of the Dharma, they made their request.
Vajragarbha, having seen them, looked out toward the four directions.
From a voice harmonious and elegant, he smiled and said:
"You sons of the Buddhas, listen all with one mind:
the meditative realm of the yogin is profound and inconceivable."
Not known through discursive thought, its concentration and object are likewise so.
Free from desire and unwholesome states, as well as all forms of distraction,
accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, joy, and bliss, one enters the tranquil first dhyāna.
In this manner, gradually and in succession, from four, eight, up to ten.
Those non-Buddhists who cling to a self constantly practice this concentration;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do likewise.

Each one knows that within the world, the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena are such that the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) are like empty villages; all are devoid of self.
They are without thought and without activity, arising merely through the conjunction of the three.
Like a mechanical corpse that has been raised, there is originally no agent who can act.
When followers of external paths cultivate this concentration, they give rise to the view of emptiness;
such people are deluded regarding the characteristics of phenomena and destroy all dharmas.

If one cultivates the sublime concentration of the Buddha, And skillfully understands that the aggregates are without self, Then one immediately gives rise to a supreme mass of merit And eliminates all erroneous views.
All things are but mind alone; There is neither the grasper nor the grasped.
There are no elements (*dhātu*) and no aggregates (*skandha*); all things are without marks (*animitta*).
Even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, these have no place of abiding.
It is through the false conceptualization of the foolish that the natures of earth, water, and so forth are [imagined].
Those who do not know its nature grasp at such signs—
wondrous forms and foul forms, as well as other appearances resembling form.
They are like rainbows and halos in the sky, or the myriad colors of clouds and mists.
One contemplates them as a skeleton pervading the entire world;
likewise, through the meditations on the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one contemplates the great elements and so forth.
Whether the body possesses form or is formless, the practitioner in meditative concentration should always contemplate with clarity.
If one is single-minded regarding an object, that very object is said to be pure;
according to how it is conceptualized, that [conceptualization] becomes the object of perception.
What is neither fixed nor fixed by anyone is falsely imagined to be fixed.
The one established in meditative concentration, while within that concentration, realizes that the world is entirely the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna);
thus, phenomena and all their characteristics are entirely eliminated.
Having attained supreme concentration, they skillfully explain all forms of meditative absorption.
They destroy those who practice meditative concentration and the dharmas known through false wisdom.
If a person possesses inferior intelligence, they grasp at phenomena and a self,
claiming their own words to be truthful and skillfully explaining all dharmas.
Attached to the characteristics of all phenomena, one destroys oneself and destroys others;
there is neither the characteristic nor the characterized, yet one falsely gives rise to views of differentiation.
Sweetness can remove heat; bitterness, sourness, saltiness, pungency, and blandness [likewise function].
The pungent taste eliminates cold; the salty can cure wind disorders.
Because of the transformation of yellow phlegm, malaria arises;
sometimes it is caused by wind alone, or by the combination of all three.
Since diseases have their distinctions, the ancient seers devised various remedies:
the six types beginning with rock honey, along with sugar and various other flavors,
are able to eliminate the manifold malarial fevers within the bodies of sentient beings.
If phenomena possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
then medicine would lack the power to eliminate disease, and the patient would never recover.
How is it that everyone in the world perceives the elimination of disease through taking medicine?
The one established in meditative concentration understands that the world is nothing but the ālayavijñāna, which undergoes transformation and continues in succession, like various illusory animals.
There is neither the grasper nor the grasped; there are no aggregates, nor is there one who possesses the aggregates.
There is neither the quality of having parts nor that of being composed of parts;
in the world there is no agent, nor is there anything produced.
There is no accumulation of dust in the world, and no one who goes to any place or direction.
Without beginning and most subtle, it gradually increases to the measure of one finger,
and even up to three fingers; as the precious substances further combine,
their distinct qualities (*guṇa*) are differentiated— yet none of these meanings truly exist.
The world is not created by Primal Nature (Prakṛti), nor can it be produced by Time;
nor is it of the nature of desire, nor is it the work of the three qualities (guṇas).
Nor does it exist without a cause, nor does it arise spontaneously.
Due to the habitual tendencies of this karma, the inner mind is agitated and turbid.
Depending on the mind and the visual faculty, various false discriminations arise;
through the mental faculty and the mental consciousness, sentient beings [possess] the ālaya-vijñāna.
Manifesting universally throughout the world, Like a magician creating illusions.
If one can enter into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), Then one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
If one speaks of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), Then one knows that marks are but consciousness.
Vases and the like have no objective reality; their substance and characteristics are all created by the mind.
What is not a vase appears as a vase; therefore, it is said to be empty.
All forms in the world, including the palaces of the various devas, [are likewise so].
All transformations that are perceptible are the ālayavijñāna.
Whatever belongs to the body of a sentient being— from the head down to the hands and feet—
whether arising all at once or gradually, there is nothing that is not the ālayavijñāna.
The habitual tendencies turbid the mind, such that ordinary fools cannot comprehend it;
this nature is neither existent, nor is it empty.
It is like a person who, with various objects, strikes and breaks a jar or the like.
If objects were empty, there would be neither subject nor object to be refuted.
My pride is like Mount Sumeru; this view does not yet constitute an obstacle.
But to be conceited and attached to emptiness—this evil exceeds even that.
Abide in what is appropriate; do not speak inappropriately.
If one expounds in an inappropriate manner, the nectar of immortality becomes poison.
All sentient beings give rise to various views.
Desiring to cause the severance of all views, Therefore, the principle of emptiness is taught.
If one hears of emptiness yet clings to it as real, One cannot sever all views;
this view cannot be removed, Just like a cataract that has been abandoned by a physician.
Just as fire burns wood, and when the wood is exhausted the fire does not remain,
so too, when one perceives that the wood has been burned, the fire of emptiness should likewise cease.
When all views are extinguished, the fire of wisdom is born.
Universally burning the fuel of afflictions, all things are rendered pure.
By means of this wisdom, the Muni is liberated within the Guhyasamāja;
he does not perceive the horns of a rabbit striking and shattering a great mountain.
There has never been a stone-child who, grasping an arrow, shot at an object;
nor have we ever heard of one wishing to engage in battle while seeking a bow made of hare-horns.
How could there be a stone-child capable of constructing a palace?
The emptiness of all phenomena is eternally of one essence with those phenomena.
From the moment of conception in the womb, when form arises, it immediately perishes;
there is no perishing apart from emptiness, and there is no emptiness apart from form.
Just as the moon and its radiance are never different from beginning to end,
so too are all phenomena: emptiness and [the phenomena] are one,
mutually indistinguishable, and thus whatever is undertaken is accomplished.
This body is like a corpse; from the beginning it lacks intrinsic nature.
Bound by the ropes of craving and pulled about by sensory objects, one speaks of the subtle principle of emptiness in order to purify all views.
Those who possess wisdom should study with single-minded devotion.
Just as a skilled illusionist, by the power of various incantations and arts,
creates all manner of things from grasses and trees according to his will.
Depending upon the sense faculties and craving, and upon visible forms, light, and mental attention, consciousness arises;
it is devoid of reality, like a magical illusion or a mirage.
This consciousness has no place from which it comes, nor does it go to any other direction.
The nature of all consciousnesses is likewise thus: they neither exist nor do they not exist, and one should not cling to them as changing.
Like a net of hair, a rabbit's horn, or the son of a barren woman, they have no essence from the very beginning; names are falsely established for them.
Lions, tigers, bears, and brown bears; horses, donkeys, and camels;
crocodiles, turtles, and tortoises—none of these possess horns.
Why do you not distinguish them in this way, but speak only of the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn?
How could the Supreme Speaker not establish [the truth]?
He reveals it for the sake of the wise; it is only their own false conceptualization.
The multitudes of non-Buddhists are deluded, like those who are mute, deaf, and blind.
They possess no wisdom for transcendence, nor do they have the Dharma realized within;
they merely follow the shifting words of others—what use is there in such discrimination?
If one falsely gives rise to discrimination, one will not be born in Ghanavyūha.
Those who possess meditative concentration attain the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) and are able to be born in this realm.
Just as the celestial palaces, the sun, the moon, and the myriad stars revolve around Mount Sumeru, all turning by the power of the wind; so too do these beings abide.
The seven consciousnesses are likewise; relying upon the ālayavijñāna, sustained by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they perpetually circulate everywhere.
Just as relying upon the great earth, the various kinds of plants and trees can grow,
All sentient beings, And even all manner of precious jewels;
Such is the ālayavijñāna, The support upon which all consciousnesses depend.
It is like a peacock bird, Whose feathers possess many brilliant colors.
Male and female love one another, dancing and frolicking together in joy;
so too are the ālaya, its seeds, and all phenomena,
which abide in mutual dependence— one who is concentrated is able to perceive this.
Just as the hundreds of rivers flow, day and night returning to the great ocean,
their currents never ceasing, yet the ocean makes no discrimination;
so too is the ālayavijñāna, profound and without limit or bottom.
The habitual tendencies of the various consciousnesses constantly flow toward it day and night.
Just as the earth contains manifold treasures with diverse colors and forms,
which sentient beings enjoy according to what they attract through their merit;
Thus the ālayavijñāna, accompanied by various conceptualizations, increases birth and death;
through the transformation of the basis, it becomes perfect awakening.
By skillfully cultivating pure conduct, one transcends the ten stages.
Entering into the stage of Buddhahood, The ten powers are all perfected;
Abiding correctly in the limit of reality, Constantly and eternally indestructible,
Manifesting various transformations, Like the earth, without discrimination.
Just as the colors of various flowers in spring are joyfully admired by both humans and birds, so too is the *ādāna-vijñāna*;
yet those established in meditative concentration are often deluded regarding its grasping.
Thus, O Sons of the Buddha, those who lack wisdom remain separated from reality.
Lacking skillful knowledge of the meaning, they utter false words with dogmatic certainty;
through unrighteous speech that sows discord, they deceive and delude sentient beings.
While all phenomena abide in their distinctness, they nevertheless give rise to divisive discourse.
Just as a skilled illusionist, Proficient in the use of incantations,
Manifests various kinds of flowers, Yet those flowers, fruits, and seeds do not exist; So too,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Through their skillful wisdom and expedient means,
The world dwells in diversity, and through diverse manifestations,
various gates of teaching are proclaimed; these endless exhortations and instructions reveal the definitive,
true Dharma, which appears within the Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja).
The six elements and eighteen, the twelve bases, and the person—
drawn by the tether of the mind, sentient beings wander through saṃsāra.
The eight consciousnesses, the various elements, and the bases arise together in harmony.
Driven by the rope of the mind, the preceding body passes on to the subsequent body.
This transmigrating person (*puruṣa*) manifests according to worldly causes;
as this single embodied being, he continues through successive births without interruption.
The six elements and the person, as well as the twelve bases and the eighteen elements—
the mental activities— are said to belong to the Sovereign.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha...
Having finished explaining the meaning of the "Great Man" (puruṣa) regarding the elements (dhātu) and sense-fields (āyatana),
all the fearless sons of the Buddha bowed their heads in prostration before the Maṇi-jewel treasury palace in the Pure Abode of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from other directions who have come to reside in this assembly all join their voices together and praise, saying, "Excellent!
Furthermore, there are various Bodhisattvas, as well as devas and devīs.
With palms joined and minds unified in reverence, they looked upon one another and spoke these words:
"Excellent is your exposition for the sake of all bodhisattvas on the meaning of the 'Sublime Hero'."
Far removed from the treatises of non-Buddhists,
the pure person of the six elements is merely a combination of these elements,
flowing and turning according to causes.
"Just as the tracks of various flying birds appear in the sky,
and just as fire blazes forth when separated from wood—
so too are bird-tracks seen in the air, and fire exists apart from wood."
Neither I nor any in the world have ever seen such a thing:
when a bird flies upon its wings, there is no trace left in the sky.
When you, O Venerable One, speak of the *puruṣa*, it is like the tracks of a bird.
How is it that within the various realms of existence, the principle of saṃsāra is established?
Why do you speak of a "person" (pudgala) who constantly transmigrates through birth and death,
experiencing the fruits of pleasure and pain, such that the karma one has performed is never lost?
Just as when a farmer performs his work, the labor will certainly not be in vain;
once this fruit has matured, it can produce a subsequent fruit.
So too, one who practices wholesome deeds within the body, [will experience their results].
In successive births and future lives, one will constantly enjoy the pleasures of gods and humans.
By always cultivating merit and virtue, one gathers the provisions that serve as the cause for Buddhahood;
through liberation and the various perfections, one achieves unsurpassed enlightenment.
The fruit of sovereignty in rebirth in heaven is attained through contemplative practice that perceives the true self.
Apart from the person who transmigrates, nothing at all exists.
Regarding karma and its retribution, what is done is never lost in vain.
From the Avīci Hell below, up to the various heavens above,
those called "beings" and "persons" transmigrate through birth and death.
Within all the worlds, both internal and external, seeds and manifestations give rise to sprouts and fruits.
This dharma resembles that; that arises from this.
If there were one who undergoes saṃsāra apart from the person (pudgala), it would be like saying that the daughter of a barren woman advances and retreats with dignified deportment.
Rabbit horns possess sharpness; oil can be extracted from sand.
After the bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the devas and devīs, had spoken these words, they made offerings to the One Worthy of Offerings.
Then the Honored One Vajragarbha, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, having completed the acts of offering, spoke these words in unison:
"The Eye of Dharma is complete and without deficiency; its causes and metaphors are all adorned."
Able to crush all heterodox arguments and the faults of the various schools of non-Buddhists,
having already subdued others, you now reveal your own school;
therefore, O Great Hero, you should swiftly expound it.
"We all wish to hear this; may the one of Great Wisdom speak.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, hearing the earnest request of the devas, immediately addressed them, saying:
“You gods and humans, listen with single-minded attention:
this Dharma is profound and inconceivable, beyond the reach of discursive analysis.
The principles of pure yoga are here unfolded through causes and analogies.”
I now manifest within the Guhyasamāja, and shall now proclaim it for you:
the Guhyasamāja is most subtle and wondrous, the supreme abode of those in meditative concentration.
When Vajragarbha had spoken these words, [he continued:]
He further addressed the great tree, the King of the Kinnaras, saying:
"O Great Tree, King of the Kinnaras!
You should examine: what is the nature of all phenomena?"
The nature of things is empty and non-existent;
seeing thus in accordance with reality, one is not deluded regarding meditative concentration.
Just as when a single grain of rice is cooked, the condition of the remaining grains can be known.
All phenomena are likewise so; by knowing one, one knows them all.
Just as one who churns curd tastes it with the tip of a finger, so too can the nature of all phenomena be observed through a single [instance].
"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither existent, nor is it empty;
it is the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the storehouse takes emptiness as its characteristic.
At that moment, the King of the Mahādruma Kinnaras asked:
"How can there be realms and persons within the measure of mind?
How do the various realms arise—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha [spoke].
