Having heard what he had said, [the Buddha] spoke these words:
"Excellent, O Great King of Trees!
May those who cultivate meditative concentration attain the realization of ultimate reality."
I shall now speak for you; lute master, listen attentively.
In the past, you and your retinue, having transformed yourselves and others, came through the air with drums and music, riding upon a precious palace.
Thus these celestial hosts, together proceeding to the Buddha’s assembly, played exquisite jewel lutes; their sounds were most harmonious and elegant.
Those śrāvakas present in the assembly each said to one another:
“I delight to behold the King of Trees, where the hosts of kinnaras sport,
and their palaces upon which they ride, adorned with exquisite jewels.
You play the lapis lazuli lute, causing the hearts of all to be moved with joy.”
Kāśyapa and the other śrāvakas, unaware of themselves, rose and began to dance;
moved by the exquisite harmony of the music, they were unable to maintain their original composure.
Then the Bodhisattva Tiara-Adorned addressed Kāśyapa and the others, saying:
“You who have abandoned desire, why do you dance and play?
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed that celestial crown-wearer:
“The Son of the Buddha possesses great power, like the Vairambha wind.”
The śrāvakas lack stable wisdom; like the Black Mountains, they are subject to movement.
Though they have abandoned the conceptualization of delusions, they remain stained by the mire of habitual tendencies.
Having partially realized the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they have not yet severed all latent propensities.
If you abandon all coarse heaviness, you will surely attain enlightenment.
Regarding subtle objects, you possess skillful wisdom and mastery of all treatises;
as a world-renowned light equal to Śakra, you have attained thorough penetration into those teachings.
And the treatises of the kiṃnaras, the Tathāgata’s pure principle,
and his skill regarding the characteristics of the various stages— clearly understanding and being certain of these—
he sits upright within the precious palace, surrounded by his retinue.
Radiant, pure, and exquisitely adorned, like the full moon at its peak;
having attained mastery through contemplative practice, he is able to engage in dialogue amidst the assembly.
When asked by me, "O Great Being, how does the realm arise from the mind? [he replied:]
You and all you sons of the Buddha, should all listen with a single mind.
Just as within all realms, that which is called "mind" is termed the "Great Man," and all realms arise because of it— I shall now explain this meaning.
Moisture arises from water; intense heat arises from fire.
All various movements and activities arise from this, giving rise to the wind element.
From the demarcation of form, there exist space and earth.
Consciousness and its various objects, along with habitual tendencies, are able to produce the body.
The eye, visible forms, and so forth—each with its distinct characteristics—are made into gateways where there is no gateway; thus, all states of existence are constantly continuous.
At that time, from the palace of sovereign power, the treasury of mani jewels,
the Great Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, together with all the most excellent sons of the Victor,
rose simultaneously from their seats, prostrated themselves, and paid homage.
Each holding exquisite offerings, they made worship to Vajragarbha;
covering him with nets of jewels, they praised the Buddha with one voice:
“O Noble One, you dwell securely upon the Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma.”
Having entered the realm of the Tathāgata, his manifestations are truly immeasurable;
he is able to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to all the great beings.
At that time, the Kinnara King, together with his various court ladies and others, [paid homage].
They made offerings and offered praise:
“A mani-jewel palace, a pure and sublime place of practice— For our sake,
may you expound The subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata.”

At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ṛddhiprabhāsa, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhin— Please note: The term *Ṛddhiprabhāsa* (神通王) has been translated as "King of Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhiprabhāsa*), though it may also be interpreted as "King of Spiritual Powers.
The name *Ratnaśikhin* (寶髻) is rendered here as "Jewel-Crested. The names provided reflect standard Sanskrit reconstructions based on the Chinese transliterations.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Heavenly Crown (Dharmacakrapravartin), the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sovereign of Totality (Dhāraṇīśvara-rāja),
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Accomplisher of All Meanings (Sarvārthasiddha)— these and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
as well as countless others who have cultivated sublime meditative concentrations, are all sons of the Buddha; they possess sovereign majestic power and are definitively fearless.
Skillfully able to reveal the mind of contemplative practice, they all rose from their seats, looked at one another,
and questioned the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
speaking in verse: "O Sovereign Vajra, you are able to reveal the Dharma-eye;
Sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas all revere and look up to them;
having skillfully mastered the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), they are adept at their establishment.
The Sons of the Buddha, a host of great power, with one mind all offer this exhortation.
O King of Samādhi, may you take pity on us and reveal within the Ghanavyūha the profound and marvelous matters concerning the Buddhas and their sons;
for this Dharma is most pure and utterly transcends all verbal expression.
The emanation-buddhas and various bodhisattvas, who have never before been fully blossomed,
practice through the wisdom of self-awakening; they behold the true, untainted realm,
the subtle and wondrous bliss of the present dharma— pure and most peerless.
Possessing all samādhis and immeasurable dhāraṇīs,
The various masteries and liberations, The ten kinds of mind-made bodies,
And the supreme purity of form, They illuminate the entire dharma-realm.
The inconceivable Sugata adorns his lands in this same way;
the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas have bodies the size of a subtle atom,
or even as small as a single hair-tip divided into a hundred parts.
The Guhyasamāja-vimala realm is the most excellent among all lands.
Such practitioners of contemplation all come to be born therein;
what is the cause for this?
"O Son of the Buddha, please proclaim it!
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
whose body was like a lion’s chest and who was endowed with the thirty-two marks, [spoke].
Adorned with the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), he was about to reveal [the teaching] extensively;
observing that great assembly like a lion king,
he knew the multitude was capable of hearing it— the secret intent of the Buddhas of antiquity.
I now expound the Dharma-eye, which is free from subject and object of cognition.
Vajragarbha then uttered a pure Brahma-voice,
a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, and a voice with the mark of the broad and long tongue.
A voice that is skillful and free from coarseness; A voice praised by the world;
A voice that is beautiful, expansive, and fluent; A voice perfectly attuned to the musical scales;
A voice with lofty tones that are clear and penetrating; A voice like that of the Gandharvas.
The heroic voice and the upright voice, the Kāśika-like plaintive voice,
the voice harmonizing with song, the rapid voice and the slow voice,
and the deep, far-reaching, and melodious voice— all these are fully possessed.
Through the correspondence of all virtues, Upon hearing them, one becomes free from attachment;
The mind never experiences weariness, And all find joy and delight.
One is able to fully penetrate and comprehend All characteristics of sound and voice.
Spontaneously and universally responding, Without action or effort.
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha Has never spoken a word with his mouth;
All his various sounds arise Exclusively through the power of his original vows.
From his brows, forehead, and crown, from the tip of his nose, his shoulders, and his knees—
just like a miraculous transformation— spontaneously issued forth sublime sounds,
universally revealing the Eye of Dharma for the great assembly.
The valiant Vajragarbha dwells in the Palace of Sovereignty,
surrounded by the most excellent sons; pure and immaculate,
he is like a king of swans upon the earth, attended by a flock of swans.
The Great Vajragarbha, seated upon the lion throne, outshines all practitioners,
like the moon in the sky, its light illuminating the array of stars.
Just as the moon and its radiance are without distinction,
so too is the majestic power of Vajragarbha no different from that of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s great power was seen as it truly is.
The most supreme among all practices, abiding in the path of yoga,
he rose from his seat and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"How marvelous is the Mahāyāna Dharma, the subtle and wondrous realm of the Tathāgata!"
In all Buddha-lands, the sons of the Buddhas should pay homage.
The inconceivable and stainless Dharma, which all Buddhas contemplate,
is rare, most subtle, and profound— the pure principle of the Mahāyāna.
It is not the realm of unwholesome discursive thought, but the wondrous path of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The distinctions among the eight consciousnesses, the differences between the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
and the five dharmas and two kinds of selflessness— each of these is revealed.
The five kinds of habitual objects give rise to all manner of false discriminations;
yet upon seeing this subtle and wondrous Dharma, one becomes pure like genuine gold.
Those who attain true nature abide within the lineage of the Buddhas.

The nature of the Tathāgata is subtle and wondrous; transcending the Śrāvakas and non-Buddhists, it is the supreme realm of the Guhyasamāja (Ghanavyūha). Only those who have realized it can go there, O Venerable Vajragarbha!
"What samādhi has been attained?
Regarding the pure Dharma-eye you have spoken of, what is the objective realm of that samādhi?
At that time, immeasurable bodhisattvas again prostrated to Vajragarbha:
"O Great Wisdom Vajra Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us:
abiding in which samādhi are you able to teach this Dharma?
All these sons of the Buddha desire to hear it."
At that time, Vajragarbha, dwelling in his sovereign palace, surveyed the great assembly and thought to himself:
"This Dharma is inconceivable; it is the subtle and wondrous realm of the Ten Powers."
Sustained by wisdom, they are capable of receiving [the teaching] while remaining detached from it.
To those who have seen [the truth] and are capable of abiding [in it], all the sons of the Buddhas immediately address them, saying:
"Listen attentively, all of you; I shall now explain for your sake the sublime path of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
For the sake of the sons of the Buddhas and the hosts of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin deities, I have attained the samādhi named 'The Accomplishment of Virtue in the Mahāyāna.'"
Abiding in this samādhi, they manifest the pure Dharma-eye and see billions of dust-like lands; all the Sugatas therein,
numbering as many as nayutas of billions of dust motes, stand before them and offer praise:
"Excellent is what you have spoken; this is the path of yoga.
We shall all practice it, and through such samādhi, we shall attain mastery and achieve pure, perfect enlightenment."
All Buddhas of the ten directions arise from this samādhi;
know it to be most supreme, beyond the reach of discursive thought.
If there are bodhisattvas who dwell within this samādhi, [they shall attain such excellence].
Abiding thus in the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas,
one realizes the sphere of one's own wisdom and beholds the Buddhas of samādhi manifesting hundreds of thousands of billions of transformations, even as numerous as motes of dust.
The realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization is that which all Buddhas have established;
this Dharma is devoid of all characteristics and is far removed from sound and form.
Names arise from characteristics, and characteristics arise from causes and conditions.
These two give rise to conceptualization; the nature of all phenomena is suchness (tathatā).
To observe this skillfully is called right knowledge.
This is termed the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva); its characteristics are the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Far removed from names and signs—this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) dwells within the body, flowing and circulating according to circumstances;
its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are heaped up like mountains, entangled by profound meanings.
The seeker of the Dharma has two gates: the mental consciousness arises simultaneously with the five sense objects manifesting before one; thus the various bodies of consciousness are in harmony.
It is as if there were a self or a person dwelling within the body.
The ālayavijñāna is like a violent torrent of water, tossed by the winds of objective spheres.
Various waves of consciousness arise, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Only the Buddhas and their sons can realize that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature.
Having already attained the state of a Tathāgata, he further proclaims it for the sake of others.
By analyzing the teaching on the aggregates, one perceives the selflessness of persons;
yet not knowing the selflessness of phenomena, such a person is called a śrāvaka.
The practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas lead to a thorough realization of the two kinds of selflessness;
having contemplated this, they immediately relinquish [grasping], yet do not abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
If one were to abide in the limit of reality, one would then abandon the mind of great compassion.
All his meritorious deeds would remain unfulfilled, and he could not attain perfect enlightenment.
With rare and inconceivable wisdom, he universally benefits all sentient beings;
like a lotus emerging from the mud, his physical form is most majestic and pure.
The devas and noble sages, upon seeing them, give rise to love and reverence.
Thus do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge from the mire of birth and death;
having attained the pure body of Buddhahood, they are the object of the devas' joyful veneration.
From the initial stage of a bodhisattva, whether acting as a wheel-turning monarch,
a lord of the gandharvas, or a king of the asuras,
having fully realized the Mahāyāna Dharma, one attains such a body as this.
By practicing in gradual stages, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, all sons of the Buddha should study with a single mind:
all phenomena that are defiled, as well as those that are pure.
Throughout the cycle of birth and death, all things revolve because of the ālayavijñāna.
This cause is supreme and peerless; it is proclaimed by those who have realized the truth.
It is not like the "efficient cause" (kartṛ) or similar concepts such as an "autonomous creator" (īśvara).
The World-Honored One spoke of this consciousness To eliminate all habitual tendencies;
To realize its ultimate purity, The ālayavijñāna cannot be apprehended.
If the ālayavijñāna were apprehendable, Purity would not be eternal.
The Tathāgata’s pure treasury is also called stainless wisdom;
it abides eternally without beginning or end, transcending the discourse of the four extremes.
The Buddha taught that the tathāgatagarbha is the ālayavijñāna.
Those of evil wisdom cannot know that the *tathāgatagarbha* is none other than the *ālayavijñāna*.
The Tathāgata’s pure store and the worldly *ālaya* are,
like gold and a finger-ring, mutually indistinguishable.
Just as a skilled goldsmith, using pure and fine gold,
fashions a finger ornament intended to adorn the finger,
its appearance distinct from other objects, which is called a ring.
The noble ones who experience happiness in the present life realize the domain of self-awakened wisdom;
their virtues increase ever more excellently, beyond what can be described by themselves or others.
Those practitioners of meditative concentration in the present life thoroughly comprehend that objects are but mind alone.
Upon attaining the seventh stage, all objects of perception for the mind and consciousness—
every external realm and the perception of various distinctions— are completely transformed and extinguished; there is no objective world, but only mind alone.
The various illusions of jars, garments, and the like—none of these exist at all;
yet as transformations of the mind, they appear as such, with a grasper and a grasped.
Just as the stars and the moon move in dependence upon Mount Sumeru, so too do these appearances arise.
So too it is with all the consciousnesses, Which always evolve in dependence upon the ālaya.
The ālaya is the Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha); Its wondrous essence is fundamentally pure.
Without mind and without cognition, It is as radiant and pure as refined gold.
It cannot be differentiated; its nature is free from conceptual construction.
Its essence is truly the perfected nature—this is what the yogi should perceive.
When the mental consciousness conditions an object, it merely binds the fool.
"The noble vision is entirely pure, Just like a mirage and the like.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Vajragarbha, along with the assembly of beings as numerous as motes of dust who had come from other directions to this gathering, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
